entries.shortExplanation: N이에요 / 예요 means "to be / am / is / are" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N이에요 / 예요 (N-ieyo / yeyo) means "to be / am / is / are" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 학생이에요 ("I am a student."). Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Use this for identity, names, jobs, places, and simple “it is...” sentences. It does not describe actions.

patternInfo.formNote: Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.

entries.shortExplanation: N 주세요 means "please give me N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N 주세요 (N juseyo) means "please give me N" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 물 주세요 ("Water, please."). Use for ordering or asking for an item. Add 좀 when you want the request to sound a little softer.

entries.shortExplanation: 못 + verb means "cannot / be unable to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "cannot / be unable to" uses the pattern 못 + verb (mot + verb). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 못 가요 ("I cannot go."). For most verbs, put 못 before the normal verb form: 가요 becomes 못 가요. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요. Never make forms like 못 가해요.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.
entries.contextHint: Use it for inability, schedule conflicts, food restrictions, or language limits: 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 한국어를 잘 못해요. It says “I cannot” because of a real limit, not simply “I choose not to.”

patternInfo.formNote: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal verb form: 가요 becomes 못 가요. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요. Never make forms like 못 가해요.

studyGuide.title: Cannot / unable to
howToBuild: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal polite verb: 가요 becomes 못 가요, 먹어요 becomes 못 먹어요.
Do not add 해요 to a non-하다 verb. It is 못 가요, not 못 가해요.
For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요: 해요 becomes 못 해요, 공부해요 becomes 공부 못 해요.
studyGuide.whenToUse: Use it for inability, schedule conflicts, food restrictions, or language limits: 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 한국어를 잘 못해요. It says “I cannot” because of a real limit, not simply “I choose not to.”

entries.shortExplanation: V/A-잖아요 means "you know (shared/obvious reason)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-잖아요 (-janayo) = "you know (shared/obvious reason)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 내가 어제 말했잖아. ("I told you yesterday, remember."). Attach 잖아(요) straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; there is no 으 buffer, so a final consonant changes nothing (많다 to 많잖아요). For past events use 았/었잖아요 (말했잖아요), and a noun adds 이잖아요 / 잖아요 (주말이잖아요, 친구잖아요). The core job is to remind the listener of a fact you both already share, almost like saying 'come on, you know this' — it flags the reason as common ground rather than new news. Because it presumes the other person should already know, leaning on it too hard sounds mildly accusatory ('I already TOLD you'), which is why it is a friends-and-close-coworkers ending with no true 합니다 form. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for it to deliver fresh information ('나 어제 이사했잖아요' to someone who never knew you moved) — that lands as a passive-aggressive scold; for genuinely new background you want 거든요 instead.

entries.nuance: Attach 잖아(요) straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; there is no 으 buffer, so a final consonant changes nothing (많다 to 많잖아요). For past events use 았/었잖아요 (말했잖아요), and a noun adds 이잖아요 / 잖아요 (주말이잖아요, 친구잖아요). The core job is to remind the listener of a fact you both already share, almost like saying 'come on, you know this' — it flags the reason as common ground rather than new news. Because it presumes the other person should already know, leaning on it too hard sounds mildly accusatory ('I already TOLD you'), which is why it is a friends-and-close-coworkers ending with no true 합니다 form. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for it to deliver fresh information ('나 어제 이사했잖아요' to someone who never knew you moved) — that lands as a passive-aggressive scold; for genuinely new background you want 거든요 instead.
commonMistakes: English speakers use 잖아요 to break news ('우리 헤어졌잖아요' to someone who didn't know) — but it presumes shared knowledge, so it sounds like a scolding 'as you should know.' For info the listener lacks, switch to 거든요 (헤어졌거든요).
Don't aim it at elders or strangers; even with 요 the 'you already know this' flavor reads as naggy or rude. Reserve it for friends and close colleagues, and soften with a gentle, not falling, tone.
It is not a yes/no question marker. 비싸잖아요? to ask 'isn't it expensive?' is unnatural — for confirmation use 비싸지 않아요? or 비싸죠?.

entries.shortExplanation: V/A-거든요 means "(it's) because / here's the thing" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-거든요 (-geodeunyo) means "(it's) because / here's the thing" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 저 오늘 못 가요. 약속이 있거든요. ("I can't come today. I have plans, see."). Add 거든(요) to a plain verb or adjective stem with no 으 buffer (작다 to 작거든요); past uses 았/었거든요 (잤거든요), and a noun adds 이거든요 (학생이거든요). It supplies a reason or piece of background the listener does NOT yet have — think of it as verbally opening a parenthesis: '(the thing is...)'. It frequently answers a 왜? or sets up the next sentence of a story, and the rising-then-settling intonation invites the listener to keep listening. The single most useful contrast for learners is 거든요 vs 잖아요: 거든요 delivers NEW information ('약속이 있거든요' = you didn't know I have plans), while 잖아요 recalls SHARED information ('약속 있다고 했잖아요' = I already told you). Said with a flat, clipped falling tone to a stranger it can sound a touch defensive or self-justifying, so let the pitch stay light.

commonMistakes: The number-one error is swapping 거든요 and 잖아요. 거든요 = the listener does NOT know yet; 잖아요 = you both already know. Telling a friend who already heard the news '나 차였거든' is fine as fresh disclosure, but if they witnessed it, 차였잖아 fits.

entries.shortExplanation: V/A-더라고요 means "I noticed / it turned out (firsthand)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "I noticed / it turned out (firsthand)" uses the pattern V/A-더라고요 (-deoragoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 가 보니까 생각보다 좋더라고요. ("When I went, it was better than I thought."). Attach 더라고(요) to a plain verb or adjective stem to report something you personally witnessed, felt, or realized at an earlier moment and are now relaying — the 더 carries the meaning 'I retrieved this from my own past observation.' Crucially it marks firsthand evidence: you must have seen, heard, or directly experienced it, never merely been told. Because the discovery belongs to you, you normally avoid it for your OWN deliberate actions or feelings you already knew about (X 나 학생이더라고요), though it works beautifully for self-realizations you stumbled onto (혼자 살아 보니까 외롭더라고요 = I found out, to my surprise, that I'm lonely). Compare it with plain past 았/었어요, which just states a finished fact flatly; 더라고요 adds 'and this is what I noticed about it,' a reporter's color. The 고 is routinely dropped in speech, leaving the very casual 더라.

entries.nuance: Attach 더라고(요) to a plain verb or adjective stem to report something you personally witnessed, felt, or realized at an earlier moment and are now relaying — the 더 carries the meaning 'I retrieved this from my own past observation.' Crucially it marks firsthand evidence: you must have seen, heard, or directly experienced it, never merely been told. Because the discovery belongs to you, you normally avoid it for your OWN deliberate actions or feelings you already knew about (X 나 학생이더라고요), though it works beautifully for self-realizations you stumbled onto (혼자 살아 보니까 외롭더라고요 = I found out, to my surprise, that I'm lonely). Compare it with plain past 았/었어요, which just states a finished fact flatly; 더라고요 adds 'and this is what I noticed about it,' a reporter's color. The 고 is routinely dropped in speech, leaving the very casual 더라.
commonMistakes: Don't use 더라고요 for secondhand news you only heard. '친구가 시험 떨어졌더라고요' is odd if you weren't there — for hearsay use 떨어졌대요 (-대요). 더라고요 demands your own eyes/ears.
Avoid it for your own settled, already-known feelings or intentions: '나 너 좋아하더라고요' is wrong because you already knew. It only fits feelings you newly discovered in yourself (살아 보니 외롭더라고요).

It is past-leaning observation, so don't pair it with a clearly present-and-ongoing 'right now.' For what you see this second, use 보여요/네요 (비 와요 / 비 오네요), not 비 오더라고요, which implies you noticed it earlier.

entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ래요? means "shall we? / wanna? / will you?" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ래요? (-(eu)llaeyo) = "shall we? / wanna? / will you?". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 커피 마실래? ("Wanna grab coffee?"). Add ㄹ래요 after a vowel stem (가다 to 갈래요) and 을래요 after a consonant stem (먹다 to 먹을래요); ㄹ-final stems keep their single ㄹ and just add 래요 with no 으 buffer (놀다 to 놀래요, 만들다 to 만들래요). As a question it casually proposes doing something together or probes the listener's own will/preference; as a statement it declares your intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I feel like going). The sharp contrast to learn is ㄹ래요? vs ㄹ까요?: ㄹ까요? consults the other person's opinion on a shared plan ('shall we?', 같이 갈까요?), whereas ㄹ래요? asks what THEY personally want to do (같이 갈래요? = do you feel like going?), so it can sound a bit direct or even presumptuous to a superior. Because it centers the listener's raw will, polite as it is with 요, it is not deferential enough for a clear senior — there you upgrade to 가실래요? or 가시겠어요?.

commonMistakes: Don't fire ㄹ래요? at someone clearly above you; '부장님, 같이 갈래요?' asks the boss's bare preference and feels too forward. Upgrade to 같이 가실래요? or 같이 가시겠어요?.

entries.shortExplanation: V/A-는데요 means "soft contrast / leading-on ending" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-는데요 (-neundeyo) means "soft contrast / leading-on ending" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 지금 좀 바쁜데요. ("I'm kind of busy right now, though."). Verbs take 는데요 (가다 to 가는데요); adjectives take ㄴ데요 after a vowel (예쁘다 to 예쁜데요) and 은데요 after a consonant (좋다 to 좋은데요); 있다/없다 behave like verbs (재밌는데요) and the past for both is 았/었는데요 (재밌었는데요). Ending a sentence on 는데요 leaves the thought hanging open — it softens a statement, plants an unspoken 'but...,' or hands the conversational floor to the other person to react. Think of it as a half-finished bridge: you build the first span and let the listener walk across it. The crucial split for learners is the adjective rule: descriptive words must NOT take 는 (바쁜데요, not 바쁘는데요), because only action verbs and 있다/없다 use 는. Tonally, a trailing 는데요...? can convey surprise, mild pushback, or a polite hedge all at once depending on pitch, which is why it rarely stands fully alone with strangers without surrounding context.

entries.english: I'm planning to / I intend to
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)려고요 means "I'm planning to / I intend to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "I'm planning to / I intend to" uses the pattern V-(으)려고요 (-(eu)ryeogoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 저 일찍 자려고요. ("I'm planning to sleep early."). Add 려고요 after a vowel stem (자다 to 자려고요) and 으려고요 after a consonant stem (모으다 to 모으려고요, 찾다 to 찾으려고요) to announce your own pre-formed intention, very often as a reply to '뭐 할 거예요?'. It is the relaxed, conversational clipping of 려고 해요, with the 해요 simply left implied. The contrast you must nail is 려고 vs 으러: both involve purpose, but 으러 attaches only to a movement verb to mark the goal of going/coming (사러 가요 = I go in order to buy), while 려고 states a standalone plan/aim and pairs with any verb (사려고요 = I'm planning to buy). A second caution: 려고요 reports the speaker's intention, so it is awkward to assert flatly about someone else's plan — for a third person's apparent intent you soften to 려나 봐요 or simply ask them.

commonMistakes: Don't confuse 으려고 with 으러. Use 으러 only with go/come for the purpose of an errand (밥 먹으러 가요 = I go to eat); use 려고 for a standalone intention with any verb (밥 먹으려고요 = I'm planning to eat). '밥 먹으러요' as a full answer is wrong.
State it only about your own plans. For someone else's intention, '친구가 오려고요' sounds off — say 친구가 오려나 봐요 ('seems like my friend intends to come') or just report 온대요.
Don't graft a future ending on top: it's already forward-looking, so 자려고 할 거예요 is redundant. Say 자려고요 or, more fully, 자려고 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: V-는 중이에요 means "in the middle of doing" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 중이에요 (-neun jung-ieyo) = "in the middle of doing". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 지금 가는 중이에요. ("I'm on my way right now."). Attach 는 중이에요 to a plain verb stem to stress that an action is actively unfolding at this very moment; ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 는 (만들다 to 만드는 중이에요, 살다 to 사는 중이에요). The Sino-Korean noun 中 (중) literally means 'the middle/midst,' so 가는 중 paints 'in the very midst of going.' With a bare noun you skip the verb form and say N 중이에요 (회의 중이에요 = mid-meeting, 공사 중 = under construction). The contrast to internalize is 는 중이에요 vs plain 고 있어요: 고 있어요 broadly marks ongoing or even habitual action (요즘 한국어 배우고 있어요 = I'm learning Korean these days), while 는 중이에요 zooms in on this single moment of being mid-task and resists habitual or stretched readings. Because it needs a real unfolding action, it rejects adjectives and stative verbs like 알다/있다 — there is no 아는 중이에요.

entries.shortExplanation: V/A-나 봐요 means "seems like / I guess (from evidence)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-나 봐요 (-na bwayo) means "seems like / I guess (from evidence)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 비 오나 봐요. ("Looks like it's raining."). Verbs and 있다/없다 take 나 봐요 (오다 to 오나 봐요, 있다 to 있나 봐요); descriptive adjectives instead take ㄴ가/은가 봐요 (바쁘다 to 바쁜가 봐요, 좋다 to 좋은가 봐요), and nouns take 인가 봐요 (신입인가 봐요). The literal sense — 'I look (봐요) at whether (나)...' — captures that you are inferring from visible evidence, drawing a careful conclusion from something you observed rather than asserting it outright. The contrast learners need is 나 봐요 vs 겠어요/것 같아요: 겠어요 leans on gut feeling or general assumption (춥겠어요 = it must be cold, I imagine), and 것 같아요 is the all-purpose 'I think/seems,' while 나 봐요 specifically signals 'based on this clue in front of me, I gather...'. Since it is an outside guess, you don't apply it to your own clear feelings — 나 슬픈가 봐 (I guess I'm sad) only works as wry self-observation, never as a plain statement of how you feel.

entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 means "almost (did but didn't)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "almost (did but didn't)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 (-(eu)l ppeonhaesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 늦을 뻔했어요. ("I almost ran late."). Add ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel stem (늦다... wait, 늦다 is consonant — 넘어지다 to 넘어질 뻔했어요) and 을 뻔했어요 after a consonant stem (늦다 to 늦을 뻔했어요); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (울다 to 울 뻔했어요). It describes an event that very nearly occurred but ultimately did NOT — a near-miss or close call — and it is locked in the past tense 했어요 because the moment of almost-happening is already over. The defining nuance is the relief or alarm baked in: you escaped the outcome, so it usually pairs with a 살았다-style payoff (덕분에 살았어요, 겨우 피했어요) or a hair-raising setup. Don't confuse it with 을 것 같았어요 ('it seemed like it would'), which is a guess about likelihood; 뻔했어요 asserts the thing was a whisker away from really happening. The English trap is using it for things that DID happen — 'I almost finished' meaning you nearly completed it is NOT 끝낼 뻔했어요 (which would mean you came close but failed); for that, use 거의 끝냈어요.

entries.shortExplanation: V/A-는 척하다 means "to pretend / act as if" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V/A-는 척하다 (-neun cheokada) = "to pretend / act as if". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 자는 척했어. ("I pretended to be asleep."). Present-tense verbs take 는 척하다 (자다 to 자는 척해요); descriptive adjectives take ㄴ/은 척하다 (예쁘다 to 예쁜 척해요, 괜찮다 to 괜찮은 척해요); and a completed past action takes 은/ㄴ 척하다 (듣다 to 들은 척하다 → 안 들은 척해요). The bound noun 척 means 'a put-on pose,' so the construction literally stages an act you don't truly feel or do — you perform the outside of a state without the inside. It carries a clear undertone of falseness or insincerity, which is why it pairs naturally with 그냥, 일부러, or 안 (그냥 못 본 척했어요). The near-twin 체 (못 본 체했어요) means the same thing with a slightly bookish, old-fashioned flavor; in everyday speech 척 dominates. The English-speaker pitfall is matching the wrong modifier: 'pretend to be pretty' is 예쁜 척 (adjective form), never 예쁘는 척, and 'pretend not to hear' as a past act is 못 들은 척, not 못 듣는 척.

entries.english: I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)
entries.shortExplanation: A/V-는 것 같아요 means "I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A/V-는 것 같아요 (-neun geot gatayo) means "I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 맛있는 것 같아요 ("I think it's tasty"). Literally 'it is like the thing that...' (것 = thing/fact, 같다 = to be like/same), so you are framing your statement as a resemblance to truth rather than a flat fact — that hedge is the whole point and is why Koreans reach for it constantly. The form tracks tense on the modifier: present verb takes -는 (가는 것 같아요), adjective and past verb take -(으)ㄴ (추운 것 같아요, 먹은 것 같아요), and a future/probability guess takes -(으)ㄹ (올 것 같아요). Contrast it with the blunter guess word 같다 used as -겠- (오겠어요 'it'll surely come') and with -나 보다/-(으)ㄴ가 보다, which infer from outside evidence ('looks like, judging by what I see'); -는 것 같다 is your own soft impression, even about your own feelings (저 그 사람 좋아하는 것 같아요 = I think I like him). Register: neutral-polite and very safe, so people even soften their own opinions with it to avoid sounding pushy. The English-speaker trap is treating it as 'I think THAT (a clause)' and trying to keep a full sentence + 라고 생각해요; here the clause must be squeezed into a modifier before 것. In speech 것 almost always shrinks to 거: -는 거 같아요.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Check the situation before speaking
beginnerPath.body: Literally 'it is like the thing that...' (것 = thing/fact, 같다 = to be like/same), so you are framing your statement as a resemblance to truth rather than a flat fact — that hedge is the whole point and is why Koreans reach for it constantly. The form tracks tense on the modifier: present verb takes -는 (가는 것 같아요), adjective and past verb take -(으)ㄴ (추운 것 같아요, 먹은 것 같아요), and a future/probability guess takes -(으)ㄹ (올 것 같아요). Contrast it with the blunter guess word 같다 used as -겠- (오겠어요 'it'll surely come') and with -나 보다/-(으)ㄴ가 보다, which infer from outside evidence ('looks like, judging by what I see'); -는 것 같다 is your own soft impression, even about your own feelings (저 그 사람 좋아하는 것 같아요 = I think I like him). The English-speaker trap is treating it as 'I think THAT (a clause)' and trying to keep a full sentence + 라고 생각해요; here the clause must be squeezed into a modifier before 것. entries.english: decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)
entries.shortExplanation: V-기로 했어요 means "decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)" uses the pattern V-기로 했어요 (-giro haesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 담배 끊기로 했어요 ("I decided to quit smoking"). Here -기 turns the verb into a noun ('the doing of X') and -로 marks it as the direction/terms you settled on, so the literal feel is 'I set things toward doing X' — a resolution or an arrangement. Attach -기로 하다 straight onto any verb stem with zero sound change (운동하다 → 운동하기로, 끊다 → 끊기로), then report it in the past, 했어요, because the deciding is already done; the present 하다 (-기로 해요) reads as 'let's decide to / it's agreed that we'll', a softer proposal, which is the key contrast learners miss. Compare -(으)ㄹ게요 'I'll (promise to you, here and now)' and -(으)려고 해요 'I intend/plan to': -기로 했어요 is the firmest — a concluded decision or a mutual pact, often a New Year's resolution or a plan made with others (같이 가기로 했어요). It also commonly pairs with 약속하다 and 마음먹다. Negative puts the negation INSIDE the embedded clause — 안 V-기로 했어요 (안 가기로 했어요) or the smoother V-지 않기로 했어요 (가지 않기로 했어요); don't move 안 outside as V-기로 안 했어요, which flips the meaning to 'didn't decide to V'. English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'decided' with 결정했어요 every time — 결정하다 is heavy/formal (a board decides a policy); everyday personal resolutions overwhelmingly use -기로 했어요.

entries.english: ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief
entries.shortExplanation: V-아/어 버렸어요 means "ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-아/어 버렸어요 (-a/eo beoryeosseoyo) = "ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 다 먹어 버렸어요 ("I ended up eating it all"). 버리다 on its own means 'to throw away', and as an auxiliary it keeps that flavor: the action is done all the way, finished off, gone past the point of return — and that completeness carries emotion, either regret ('darn, I went and did it') or relief ('there, it's finally off my plate'). Build it by taking the verb's -아/어 connector and adding 버리다: stems with ㅏ/ㅗ take -아 버리다 (가다 → 가 버리다, 오다 → 와 버리다), other stems take -어 버리다 (먹다 → 먹어 버리다, 잊다 → 잊어 버리다), and 하다 → 해 버리다. Contrast its sibling -아/어 두다/놓다, which means doing something and leaving it ready ('do it in advance and keep it'), the opposite mood from 버리다's 'do it and be rid of it'; and note that 버리다 colors the feeling, while -았/었어요 alone just reports the fact. It loves 다, 그냥, 벌써 (다 먹어 버렸어요, 그냥 가 버렸어요). English-speaker pitfall: there is no English auxiliary for this, so learners drop it — but plain 다 썼어요 'I spent it all' loses the rueful punch of 다 써 버렸어요 'I went and blew it all'. Spacing matters too: write 버리다 as a separate word from the -아/어 form.

entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐요 means "I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐요 (-(eu)lkka bwayo) means "I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 늦을까 봐요 ("I'm worried I'll be late"). This is the wondering ending -(으)ㄹ까 ('I wonder if...') frozen in front of 보다 ('to see/consider'), so the literal nuance is 'considering that maybe X might happen' — and what falls out is anxiety: you are bracing for an unwanted possibility. Attach -ㄹ까 봐(요) to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈까 봐, 오다 → 올까 봐) and -을까 봐(요) to consonant stems (늦다 → 늦을까 봐, 밀리다 → 밀릴까 봐); for a worry about something already over use -았/었을까 봐요 (놓쳤을까 봐요 = worried I missed it). The sharp contrast to memorize is with the look-alike question -(으)ㄹ까요? 'shall we? / I wonder, do you think?' (갈까요? = shall we go?) — same syllables, totally different job: -ㄹ까 봐요 is never a question, it states a fear. Mid-sentence it becomes -(으)ㄹ까 봐(서) + the precaution you take because of the fear (비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요). It also pairs naturally with 걱정하다/불안하다. English-speaker pitfall: don't render 'in case' with 만약 + a conditional; 'in case it rains' is 비 올까 봐, and crucially the worry clause must describe a bad/unwanted outcome — you wouldn't use it for something you hope for.

entries.english: (someone) said that... — reporting a statement someone made
entries.shortExplanation: V-다고 했어요 means "(someone) said that... — reporting a statement someone made" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "(someone) said that... — reporting a statement someone made" uses the pattern V-다고 했어요 (-dago haesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 바쁘다고 했어요 ("He said he's busy"). This is indirect (reported) speech: -다고 quotes the content of a plain-style statement and 하다 ('to say') frames it, so you relay what someone declared without their exact words or politeness level. The endings split by word class, which is the heart of the pattern: present-tense VERBS take -ㄴ다고/-는다고 (가다 → 간다고 했어요, 먹다 → 먹는다고 했어요), but ADJECTIVES and 이다 attach plain -다고 (춥다 → 춥다고 했어요), and the past is -았/었다고 했어요 for both. Nouns use N(이)라고 했어요. The contrast that trips learners is the question version -냐고 했어요 ('asked whether...') — statements report with -다고, questions with -냐고, and mixing them is the classic reported-speech error. In casual speech everything contracts to -대(요): 간대요 (= 간다고 해요), 바쁘대 (= 바쁘다고 해), a form you'll hear far more than the full one. English-speaker pitfall: English lets you say 'He said he's busy' with a full clause and backshift the tense; Korean does NOT backshift and instead demands you re-plain-style the inner verb (그가 바쁘다고 했어요), and beginners forget that present verbs cannot stay bare -다고 — it must be -ㄴ다고/-는다고.

entries.english: (someone) asked whether/if... — reporting a question someone asked
entries.shortExplanation: V-냐고 했어요 means "(someone) asked whether/if... — reporting a question someone asked" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-냐고 했어요 (-nyago haesseoyo) = "(someone) asked whether/if... — reporting a question someone asked". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 언제 오냐고 했어요 ("They asked when I'm coming"). This is the question half of reported speech: -냐고 quotes someone's question and 하다 (or, more pointedly, 묻다/물어보다 'to ask') frames it. Modern colloquial Korean has flattened the endings, so you attach -냐고 to verb and adjective stems alike (가다 → 가냐고 했어요, 바쁘다 → 바쁘냐고 했어요); the older textbook split kept -느냐고 for verbs and -(으)냐고 for adjectives, which you'll still see in writing and in the formal 했습니다 column, but in speech -냐고 covers everything. Past is -았/었냐고 했어요, and nouns take N(이)냐고 했어요. The crucial contrast is with -다고 했어요, the STATEMENT version: a reported question must end -냐고 (오냐고 했어요 'asked if I'm coming') and a reported statement -다고 (온다고 했어요 'said he's coming') — this is the single most-confused boundary in indirect speech. Casually it contracts to -냬(요): 가냬 (= 가냐고 해), 남친 있냬 (= 있냐고 해). English-speaker pitfall: English buries the question with 'whether/if' and reorders it to statement word order ('asked WHETHER I had eaten'); Korean instead keeps the plain question intact and just clips on -냐고, and it does not switch to -다고 just because the sentence now looks declarative.

Modern colloquial Korean has flattened the endings, so you attach -냐고 to verb and adjective stems alike (가다 → 가냐고 했어요, 바쁘다 → 바쁘냐고 했어요); the older textbook split kept -느냐고 for verbs and -(으)냐고 for adjectives, which you'll still see in writing and in the formal 했습니다 column, but in speech -냐고 covers everything. Past is -았/었냐고 했어요, and nouns take N(이)냐고 했어요. The crucial contrast is with -다고 했어요, the STATEMENT version: a reported question must end -냐고 (오냐고 했어요 'asked if I'm coming') and a reported statement -다고 (온다고 했어요 'said he's coming') — this is the single most-confused boundary in indirect speech. Casually it contracts to -냬(요): 가냬 (= 가냐고 해), 남친 있냬 (= 있냐고 해). English-speaker pitfall: English buries the question with 'whether/if' and reorders it to statement word order ('asked WHETHER I had eaten'); Korean instead keeps the plain question intact and just clips on -냐고, and it does not switch to -다고 just because the sentence now looks declarative.

entries.english: it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 만해요 means "it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 만해요 (-(eu)l manhaeyo) means "it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 볼 만해요 ("It's worth watching"). 만하다 here means 'to be worth / be of a level that justifies it', so V-(으)ㄹ 만하다 says the action is worth the effort, or at least decent and tolerable — note that 'decent' often means faint praise, not glowing. Attach -ㄹ 만하다 to vowel-ending stems (보다 → 볼 만하다, 가다 → 갈 만하다) and -을 만하다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 만하다, 참다 → 참을 만하다); the past is -(으)ㄹ 만했어요. Two contrasts sharpen it: don't confuse this 만하다 (one word, 'worth doing', after -(으)ㄹ) with the size-comparison 만하다 ('as big as', as in 손바닥만 하다); and weigh it against the stronger -(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 'has real value/merit' — -(으)ㄹ 만하다 is lighter, the register of 'eh, it's worth a look' or 'edible enough'. It leans on the future-potential modifier -(으)ㄹ precisely because you're judging whether doing it would pay off. English-speaker pitfall: learners grab the present modifier -는 (보는 만해요) by analogy with 'worth watching', but the slot needs -(으)ㄹ (볼 만해요); also beware reading 먹을 만해요 as enthusiastic — to a Korean it's lukewarm, 'it'll do'.
entries.learnerPriority: First memorize two complete polite examples. Then substitute one word at a time and check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective.

entries.english: (it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice
entries.shortExplanation: V-게 됐어요 means "(it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "(it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice" uses the pattern V-게 됐어요 (-ge dwaesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 한국에 살게 됐어요 ("I ended up living in Korea"). 되다 means 'to become / come about', so V-게 되다 frames an outcome as something that turned out that way through circumstances, not pure personal will — which is exactly why it sounds humble and is the polite default for explaining how your life changed. Attach -게 되다 to any verb stem (알다 → 알게 되다, 살다 → 살게 되다) and report the result in the past, -게 됐어요 (a contraction of -게 되었어요); present/future are -게 돼요 / -게 될 거예요. The contrast to nail is against a bare past verb and against -기로 했어요: 살았어요 just states 'I lived', 살기로 했어요 says 'I (actively) decided to live (there)', while 살게 됐어요 says 'it came about that I live there' — same event, but 게 됐어요 quietly removes the spotlight from your own decision, which Koreans prefer when announcing things (회사를 그만두게 됐어요 softens 'I quit'). It often appears with 우연히, 결국, 어쩌다 보니. English-speaker pitfall: learners translate it as plain 'became' and drop 되다, collapsing 알게 됐어요 'I came to know' into 알았어요 'I knew/found out' — and they overuse the willful 결정했어요 where a modest 게 됐어요 is the socially smoother choice.

entries.english: while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 김에 means "while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ 김에 (-(eu)n gime) = "while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 나온 김에 ("while I'm out anyway"). 김 here is the noun 'occasion/opportunity created by an action', so -(으)ㄴ 김에 means 'taking advantage of the fact that you've (already) done X, also do Y' — the second clause is the real point, riding for free on the first. Attach -ㄴ 김에 to vowel-ending stems (나오다 → 나온 김에) and -은 김에 to consonant stems (씻다 → 씻은 김에); a present, ongoing action takes -는 김에 (청소하는 김에 'while I'm cleaning anyway'). The set phrase 말 나온 김에 ('since it's come up in conversation') is worth memorizing whole. Contrast it with two near-misses: -(으)면서 means doing two things simultaneously and equally ('while/as'), whereas 김에 is opportunistic and tilts toward the add-on; and -(으)니까 just gives a reason ('since/because'), without the 'might as well piggyback' flavor. English-speaker pitfall: the literal logic 'since you WILL go anyway' tempts learners to use the future -(으)ㄹ 김에, but 김에 attaches to the completed/initiated action with -(으)ㄴ (or ongoing -는) — say 가는 김에 / 나온 김에, never 갈 김에. It also pairs naturally with 이왕 ('seeing as you're at it') for extra emphasis.

entries.english: to the extent/point that... / so much that...
entries.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 정도로 means "to the extent/point that... / so much that..." as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 정도로 (-(eu)l jeongdoro) means "to the extent/point that... / so much that..." — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 죽을 정도로 피곤해요 ("I'm dead tired (tired to the point of dying)"). 정도 is the Sino-Korean noun 程度 (程 'degree' + 度 'measure'), literally 'degree/measure', so A/V-(으)ㄹ 정도로 sets a vivid 'enough-to' benchmark that conveys how intense something is — you describe a degree by naming what it could reach. Attach -ㄹ 정도로 to vowel-ending stems (아프다 → 아플 정도로) and -을 정도로 to consonant stems (죽다 → 죽을 정도로); the benchmark clause comes first and the thing being measured follows (죽을 정도로 피곤해요 = tired to the point of dying). You can also close a sentence with -(으)ㄹ 정도예요 'it's to that extent'. Contrast it with -(으)ㄹ 만큼, which is very close ('as much as / to the degree that') but more neutral/quantitative and often interchangeable, whereas -(으)ㄹ 정도로 leans expressive and is the go-to for hyperbole (죽을 정도로, 미칠 정도로); and don't confuse 정도 here with 정도 meaning 'about/approximately' (한 시간 정도 'about an hour'). It rides the future-potential modifier -(으)ㄹ because the benchmark is a hypothetical reach, not a real event. English-speaker pitfall: learners drop in the present -는 (아프는 정도로) by habit, but the slot needs -(으)ㄹ (아플 정도로); and they try to map it onto 'so ... that' word order — in Korean the 'that' clause (the degree) goes FIRST, before the predicate it modifies.

Attach -ㄹ 정도로 to vowel-ending stems (아프다 → 아플 정도로) and -을 정도로 to consonant stems (죽다 → 죽을 정도로); the benchmark clause comes first and the thing being measured follows (죽을 정도로 피곤해요 = tired to the point of dying). You can also close a sentence with -(으)ㄹ 정도예요 'it's to that extent'. Contrast it with -(으)ㄹ 만큼, which is very close ('as much as / to the degree that') but more neutral/quantitative and often interchangeable, whereas -(으)ㄹ 정도로 leans expressive and is the go-to for hyperbole (죽을 정도로, 미칠 정도로); and don't confuse 정도 here with 정도 meaning 'about/approximately' (한 시간 정도 'about an hour'). It rides the future-potential modifier -(으)ㄹ because the benchmark is a hypothetical reach, not a real event. English-speaker pitfall: learners drop in the present -는 (아프는 정도로) by habit, but the slot needs -(으)ㄹ (아플 정도로); and they try to map it onto 'so ... that' word order — in Korean the 'that' clause (the degree) goes FIRST, before the predicate it modifies.

entries.english: as much as / to the same degree as (N)
entries.shortExplanation: N만큼 means "as much as / to the same degree as (N)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "as much as / to the same degree as (N)" uses the pattern N만큼 (-mankeum). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 너만큼 잘하고 싶어요 ("I want to be as good as you"). 만큼 attaches straight onto a noun with no space and no sound change (너→너만큼, 형→형만큼, 돈→돈만큼) and sets that noun as the yardstick: 'as Adj as N.' It also rides on a verb/adjective modifier — 먹은 만큼 (as much as you ate), 노력한 만큼 (as much as you tried) — but THERE 만큼 is spaced and means 'in proportion to,' which is the dividing line learners blur: glued to a bare noun = equal degree, spaced after -은/는/을 = proportional payoff. Compare it with 처럼: 만큼 measures AMOUNT/degree ('as much as'), while 처럼 measures MANNER/likeness ('like, in the way of'), so 너처럼 means 'like you (in style)' but 너만큼 means 'to the same level as you.' The big English-speaker trap is that 만큼 has no separate word for 'as'; you do NOT add a second 'as,' and the adjective comes LAST: 너만큼 잘해 (literally 'you-as-much do-well'), never 만큼 잘해 너.

commonMistakes: Adding a leftover 'as' or fronting the adjective: English 'as good as you' tempts 만큼 잘해 너, but Korean keeps the order 너만큼 잘해 — the standard (너만큼) comes first, the predicate last, with no second 'as.'

entries.english: considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)
entries.shortExplanation: N치고 means "considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N치고 (-chigo) = "considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 초보치고 잘하네요 ("You're good for a beginner"). 치고 glues to a noun with no space (초보→초보치고, 겨울→겨울치고) and means 'measured against the norm for an N, this defies that norm' — i.e. better/worse/different than an N usually is. Add 는 → 치고는 to lean harder into the contrast (주말치고는 한산해요). The closest cousin is N에 비해 ('compared to'), but the line is sharp: 에 비해 lines up two separate things ('A에 비해 B' = relative to A, B is...), whereas 치고 stays inside ONE category and plays the member off its own stereotype ('for a beginner, surprisingly good'). There's also a flipped use — N치고 + a negative = 'there's no N that isn't...': 한국 사람치고 김치 안 먹는 사람 없어요 ('no Korean doesn't eat kimchi'); context separates the two instantly. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 치다 (to hit) — this 치고 is a fixed comparative particle, and learners wrongly try to translate 'for' with 위해 (which means 'for the sake of,' a totally different 'for').

entries.english: looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance
entries.shortExplanation: A-아/어 보이다 means "looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A-아/어 보이다 (-a/eo boida) means "looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 피곤해 보여요 ("You look tired"). Take an adjective's -아/어 form and add 보이다 (spaced): ㅏ/ㅗ stems take -아 보이다 (좋다→좋아 보이다, 작다→작아 보이다), others take -어 보이다 (힘들다→힘들어 보이다), 하다 adjectives → 해 보이다 (피곤하다→피곤해 보이다), and ㅡ-stems drop the ㅡ (예쁘다→예뻐 보이다, 바쁘다→바빠 보이다). The whole point is JUDGING BY SIGHT — 보이다 is the passive/intransitive of 보다 ('to see'), so it literally says 'X shows up as Adj to the eye.' The crucial contrast is with -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 ('seems'): 것 같다 covers ANY evidence — texts, tone, a hunch — while 아/어 보이다 is reserved for what you actually SEE, which is the exact pitfall: 'he seems busy (from his messages)' must be 바쁜 것 같아요, not 바빠 보여요. Also keep -아/어 보이다 (looks) apart from the identical-looking -아/어 보다 ('try doing'); only adjectives + 보이다 give the 'appears' meaning, while verbs + 보다 give 'attempt.'

The crucial contrast is with -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 ('seems'): 것 같다 covers ANY evidence — texts, tone, a hunch — while 아/어 보이다 is reserved for what you actually SEE, which is the exact pitfall: 'he seems busy (from his messages)' must be 바쁜 것 같아요, not 바빠 보여요. Also keep -아/어 보이다 (looks) apart from the identical-looking -아/어 보다 ('try doing'); only adjectives + 보이다 give the 'appears' meaning, while verbs + 보다 give 'attempt.'

entries.shortExplanation: N에 비해 means "compared to / in comparison with (N)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "compared to / in comparison with (N)" uses the pattern N에 비해 (-e bihae). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 작년에 비해 비싸요 ("It's expensive compared to last year"). 에 비해 attaches to a noun (작년→작년에 비해, 가격→가격에 비해) and frames 'relative to N, this is more/less...' 비해 is the -아/어 form of the Sino-Korean verb 비하다 (比하다, 比 'compare'); fuller variants are 에 비해서 (서 added, conversational) and the written/formal 에 비하여. To compare against a clause, nominalize first: V-는 것에 비해 (사는 것에 비해 = compared to living...). It overlaps with N치고 but differs sharply: 에 비해 lines up TWO separate items as a measuring stick ('A에 비해 B'), while 치고 keeps one item inside its own category ('for an N'). English-speaker pitfalls cluster here: (1) the particle is 에, not 와/하고, so 'compared TO last year' is 작년에 비해, never 작년과 비해 or 작년 비해; (2) don't substitute the everyday verb 비교하다 (比較하다, 'to compare') — the set adverbial phrase is locked as 비하다→비해, so 가격과 비교해서 is grammatical as a full verb but is NOT this fixed pattern.

entries.english: even though / despite the fact that
entries.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 means "even though / despite the fact that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 (-(eu)nde-do) = "even though / despite the fact that". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 열심히 했는데도 떨어졌어요 ("Even though I worked hard, I failed"). This is the -는데/-(으)ㄴ데 background ending plus 도 ('even'), literally 'even given the situation that...' Present verbs take -는데도 (먹다→먹는데도, 하다→하는데도); adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데도 (춥다→추운데도, 바쁘다→바쁜데도); the past for both is -았/었는데도 (잤는데도 = even though I slept); nouns take N인데도. It means 'even though X (which I'd expect to lead elsewhere), surprisingly Y.' The sharp contrast is with plain -지만 ('but'): -지만 is a flat, neutral 'but' that just joins two facts, whereas -는데도 carries the speaker's surprise or frustration that the expected consequence FAILED to follow (열심히 했지만 떨어졌어요 = 'I worked hard but failed,' a calm statement; 열심히 했는데도 떨어졌어요 = 'I worked hard and STILL failed?!', with felt letdown). English-speaker pitfall: the 'still/anyway' that English often adds in the second clause is already baked into -는데도, and the most common error is picking the wrong modifier — adjectives never take -는데도.

entries.english: only / merely (do) — nothing more than that
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 means "only / merely (do) — nothing more than that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 (-(eu)l ppun-ida) means "only / merely (do) — nothing more than that" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 할 뿐이에요 ("I'm just doing it (that's all)"). Attach -ㄹ 뿐이다 to vowel-ending stems (하다→할 뿐이다) and -을 뿐이다 to consonant stems (믿다→믿을 뿐이다); 뿐 is a bound noun, so it is spaced from the modifier. The past is -았/었을 뿐이다 (도와줬을 뿐이에요 = I only helped), and a noun takes N일 뿐이다 (친구일 뿐이에요). It pins the situation down to exactly ONE thing — 'that's all there is to it' — and is frequently defensive or modest. Watch the close rival 만 ('only'): 만 narrows the noun/object ('나만 = only ME'), but -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 narrows the whole PREDICATE/action ('I only DID, nothing else'), and the two even team up as -(으)ㄹ 뿐 (just) for emphasis. The flagship English-speaker pitfall is confusing -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 with -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라: the first CLOSES a statement off ('merely that and no more'), while the second OPENS it up ('not only that, but also'). They look almost identical but point in opposite directions.

entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 means "not only... (but also)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "not only... (but also)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 (-(eu)l ppunman anira). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 맛있을 뿐만 아니라 싸요 ("It's not only tasty but also cheap"). Attach -ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 to vowel stems (싸다→쌀 뿐만 아니라) and -을 뿐만 아니라 to consonant stems (좋다→좋을 뿐만 아니라); the past is -았/었을 뿐만 아니라. Literally it's 뿐 ('only') + 만 ('just') + 아니라 ('and not'), i.e. 'it isn't JUST that...,' so the second clause piles on something MORE, typically marked with 도 ('also'): 'not only A, but B too.' The handiest shape is the noun form N뿐만 아니라 (돈뿐만 아니라 = not only money), where 뿐만 glues onto the noun. The near-twin is -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다, which does the OPPOSITE — it shuts a statement down to one thing, while 뿐만 아니라 adds a second; one closes, one opens. A second useful contrast is N뿐만 아니라 vs N도 ('also'): 도 just tags one extra item, whereas 뿐만 아니라 explicitly says 'even beyond the obvious first thing.' English-speaker pitfall: don't separate the noun with a space (it's 돈뿐만, not 돈 뿐만), and remember the pairing 'not only A but also B' is realized with a trailing 도 in clause two, not a fronted word for 'also.'

entries.shortExplanation: V-기 위해(서) means "in order to / for the sake of (doing)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-기 위해(서) (-gi wihae(seo)) = "in order to / for the sake of (doing)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 돈을 모으기 위해 알바해요 ("I work part-time to save money"). Attach -기 위해(서) to a verb stem (모으다→모으기 위해, 합격하다→합격하기 위해); 위해서 (with 서) is conversational, 위하여 is the formal/written form. 위해 comes from the Sino-Korean verb 위하다 (爲하다, 爲 'for the sake of'). After a noun, use N을/를 위해(서) (가족→가족을 위해 = for my family). It marks a DELIBERATE, planned goal, so it reads a touch more formal and purposeful than casual -(으)려고 ('intending to'); that's the sharp contrast — -(으)려고 is everyday spoken intention and dislikes formal endings (-(으)려고 합니다 is fine, but goals on signs/resolutions prefer 위해), while -기 위해 suits written aims, mission statements, and earnest explanations. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) a NOUN needs 을/를 — 건강을 위해, never 건강 위해; (2) a VERB uses the -기 nominalizer, never the dictionary form — 모으기 위해, never 모으다 위해; (3) the subject of both clauses should match (you can't easily use 위해 to say 'so that SOMEONE ELSE does X' — for that, switch to -도록 or -게).

entries.english: as long as / so long as (a condition holds)
entries.shortExplanation: V-는 한 means "as long as / so long as (a condition holds)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 한 (-neun han) means "as long as / so long as (a condition holds)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 내가 사는 한 ("as long as I live"). Attach -는 한 to a verb stem (살다→사는 한, with ㄹ dropping before ㄴ; 있다→있는 한). This 한 is the Sino-Korean noun 限 ('limit, boundary'), so the clause literally sets 'the boundary/extent within which' the main clause stays true. It very often appears negative — V-지 않는 한 (포기하지 않는 한 = as long as you don't give up) = 'unless.' The sharp contrast is with plain -(으)면 ('if'): -(으)면 is a loose, common 'if/when' that just triggers a result, whereas -는 한 draws a firm CONDITION-BOUNDARY that must hold the whole time ('for as long as / only within the limit that'), so it feels stronger and more absolute — 비가 오면 안 가요 ('if it rains, I won't go') vs 비가 오지 않는 한 가요 ('I'll go unless it rains,' i.e. rain is the one boundary that stops me). English-speaker pitfall: this is a TIME/condition 'as long as,' not the QUANTITY 'as much as' (that's 만큼), and the literary set phrase 가능한 한 ('as far as possible') is fixed — don't read 한 as the number 'one.'

entries.english: so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)
entries.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ 나머지 means "so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)" uses the pattern A/V-(으)ㄴ 나머지 (-(eu)n nameoji). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 놀란 나머지 소리쳤어요 ("I was so startled that I screamed"). Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다→놀란 나머지, 긴장하다→긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다→기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다→참은 나머지). 나머지 normally means 'the remainder/leftover,' and here it figuratively names 'what spilled over from an extreme state' — i.e. the first clause was SO intense that it overflowed into the (usually negative or startling) result in the second. The natural rival is -아/어서 ('because'): -아/어서 states a plain, calm cause-and-effect, whereas -(으)ㄴ 나머지 dramatizes an EXTREME degree whose overflow produced an unintended result (긴장해서 실수했어요 = 'I was nervous so I slipped,' neutral; 긴장한 나머지 이름까지 까먹었어요 = 'I was SO nervous I even forgot my name,' vivid and excessive). It's somewhat literary/dramatic, shining in storytelling, news, and lively retellings rather than flat chit-chat. English-speaker pitfall: it ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a present feeling — never -는 나머지 — and the result clause should be a real, often unwanted consequence, not just any factual statement.

entries.nuance: Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다→놀란 나머지, 긴장하다→긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다→기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다→참은 나머지). 나머지 normally means 'the remainder/leftover,' and here it figuratively names 'what spilled over from an extreme state' — i.e. the first clause was SO intense that it overflowed into the (usually negative or startling) result in the second. The natural rival is -아/어서 ('because'): -아/어서 states a plain, calm cause-and-effect, whereas -(으)ㄴ 나머지 dramatizes an EXTREME degree whose overflow produced an unintended result (긴장해서 실수했어요 = 'I was nervous so I slipped,' neutral; 긴장한 나머지 이름까지 까먹었어요 = 'I was SO nervous I even forgot my name,' vivid and excessive). It's somewhat literary/dramatic, shining in storytelling, news, and lively retellings rather than flat chit-chat. English-speaker pitfall: it ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a present feeling — never -는 나머지 — and the result clause should be a real, often unwanted consequence, not just any factual statement.
commonMistakes: Using the present -는 나머지: this pattern ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a current feeling — 놀란 나머지, not 놀라는 나머지; 긴장한 나머지, not 긴장하는 나머지.
Choosing it for an everyday, calm cause: for plain 'because' use -아/어서 (긴장해서 실수했어요). Reserve -(으)ㄴ 나머지 for an EXTREME degree that overflows into an unintended/dramatic result.

Pairing it with a neutral, expected outcome: the second clause should be a striking or unwanted consequence (so-much-that...), not a flat fact — 'I was so nervous I forgot my name' fits; 'I was so nervous I prepared well' does not.

entries.english: doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)
entries.shortExplanation: V-다가 means "doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-다가 (-daga) = "doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 가다가 ("on the way (while going, then...)"). Attach -다가 straight onto any verb stem with no sound change (가다 → 가다가, 먹다 → 먹다가, 일하다 → 일하다가). The picture is: you were in the middle of action 1, and before finishing it you stopped, switched, or something else happened — so action 1 is left unfinished, often interrupted by surprise. In casual speech the 가 is dropped to just -다 (집에 가다 길 잃었어). CONTRAST with -고 나서: -다가 means the first action was cut short partway (밥 먹다가 나갔어 = stopped eating, left), whereas -고 나서 means it fully finished first (밥 먹고 나서 나갔어 = ate, then left). Also note 같은 주어 — the doer of action 1 and action 2 is normally the same person. Pitfall for English speakers: 'while' in English covers both simultaneous and interrupted action, but if two things truly happen AT THE SAME TIME with no switch (listen to music while studying), that is -(으)면서, not -다가.

entries.english: after finishing (and then, once that's done)
entries.shortExplanation: V-고 나서 means "after finishing (and then, once that's done)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-고 나서 (-go naseo) means "after finishing (and then, once that's done)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥 먹고 나서 ("after eating (it's all done)"). Attach -고 나서 to any verb stem with no sound change (먹다 → 먹고 나서, 끝나다 → 끝나고 나서, 운동하다 → 운동하고 나서). The 나다 part ('to come out / be completed') adds the feeling that action 1 is thoroughly DONE and over before action 2 starts — it stresses completion more strongly than plain -고. CONTRAST with plain -고: 손 씻고 먹어요 just lists two actions in order, but 손 씻고 나서 먹어요 spotlights 'only after the washing is fully finished do I eat.' CONTRAST with -은 후에/-은 다음에: those are interchangeable in meaning ('after'), but -고 나서 sounds more spoken and a touch more emphatic about finishing. You can swap to -고 나면 for a conditional 'once you've done X, then...' (운동하고 나면 개운해요). Pitfall: only the FINAL verb carries tense — never put -았/었 on the first clause (밥 먹고 나서, not 밥 먹었고 나서), and the subject of both clauses is normally the same person.

entries.english: while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 채로 means "while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄴ 채로 (-(eu)n chaero). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 불 켠 채로 잤어요 ("I slept with the light left on"). Add -ㄴ 채로 to vowel-ending stems (켜다 → 켠 채로) and -은 채로 to consonant-ending stems (입다 → 입은 채로, 앉다 → 앉은 채로). 채 is a noun meaning 'the state as it stands,' so the structure literally says 'in the state of having done X.' It describes doing the main action while a PRIOR state is left unchanged — you turned the light on, then left it that way and slept. The 로 is often dropped to just -(으)ㄴ 채. CONTRAST with -(으)면서: -(으)면서 is two ACTIONS at once (먹으면서 봐요 = eat while watching, both ongoing), but -(으)ㄴ 채로 freezes a finished state that simply persists (불 켠 채로 잤어요 = the turning-on already happened, the lit state just remains). CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ 상태로, which is almost identical but a touch more neutral/written; -채로 carries a faint nuance of 'and you weren't supposed to.' entries.english: because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)
entries.shortExplanation: V-는 바람에 means "because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 바람에 (-neun barame) = "because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 늦잠 자는 바람에 ("because I overslept"). Attach -는 바람에 to any verb stem (늦다 → 늦는 바람에, 놓치다 → 놓치는 바람에, 막히다 → 막히는 바람에). 바람 here is not 'wind' the weather but a noun meaning 'a sudden gust of cause/consequence,' so it frames an abrupt, unintended reason that led to a negative or surprising result. Despite the present-looking -는, it always points to a PAST cause, and the result clause sits in past tense. Because the cause is outside your control, it commonly comes off as an excuse. CONTRAST with -아서/어서: -아서 is the neutral all-purpose 'because' (good or bad, 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 just states it), while -는 바람에 adds the flavor 'and that unwelcome thing ruined it' (길이 막히는 바람에 = traffic, of all things, jammed me up). CONTRAST sharply with -덕분에 'thanks to,' which is the POSITIVE cause for a good result. Pitfall: it takes verbs only, never adjectives (no 추운 바람에), and you cannot use it for a command or suggestion in the result clause.

Despite the present-looking -는, it always points to a PAST cause, and the result clause sits in past tense. Because the cause is outside your control, it commonly comes off as an excuse. CONTRAST with -아서/어서: -아서 is the neutral all-purpose 'because' (good or bad, 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 just states it), while -는 바람에 adds the flavor 'and that unwelcome thing ruined it' (길이 막히는 바람에 = traffic, of all things, jammed me up). Pitfall: it takes verbs only, never adjectives (no 추운 바람에), and you cannot use it for a command or suggestion in the result clause.
commonMistakes: Using it for a good result — 바람에 carries a disruptive, unwelcome nuance, so for a welcome cause use -아서/어서 or -덕분에 (thanks to): 친구 덕분에 잘 끝났어요, never 친구가 도와주는 바람에 잘 끝났어요.

entries.english: it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 means "it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 (-(eu)l tende) means "it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 바쁠 텐데 ("you must be busy, but..."). Add -ㄹ 텐데 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올 텐데, 바쁘다 → 바쁠 텐데) and -을 텐데 to consonant-ending stems (좋다 → 좋을 텐데; 힘들다 drops ㄹ → 힘들 텐데). It comes from 터(예정·추측의 의존명사, 'the expected case') + -ㄴ데, so it means 'it must/should be the case that...' followed by a contrast, worry, or gentle suggestion. For a PAST guess use -았/었을 텐데 (피곤했을 텐데 = you must have been tired). It often trails off softly as a caring -ㄹ 텐데(요). CONTRAST with -ㄹ 건데, which sounds nearly the same but means 'I'm GOING to (my own plan), but' (저는 갈 건데 = I intend to go) — 텐데 is a GUESS about someone/something, not your own intention. CONTRAST with -겠지만: that is a drier 'probably... but,' while -ㄹ 텐데 leans warm and considerate, anticipating the listener's situation. Pitfall: English 'would' is ambiguous; here it is conjecture about a likely state, so don't use it for plans or promises.

entries.nuance: Add -ㄹ 텐데 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올 텐데, 바쁘다 → 바쁠 텐데) and -을 텐데 to consonant-ending stems (좋다 → 좋을 텐데; 힘들다 drops ㄹ → 힘들 텐데). It comes from 터(예정·추측의 의존명사, 'the expected case') + -ㄴ데, so it means 'it must/should be the case that...' followed by a contrast, worry, or gentle suggestion. For a PAST guess use -았/었을 텐데 (피곤했을 텐데 = you must have been tired). It often trails off softly as a caring -ㄹ 텐데(요). CONTRAST with -ㄹ 건데, which sounds nearly the same but means 'I'm GOING to (my own plan), but' (저는 갈 건데 = I intend to go) — 텐데 is a GUESS about someone/something, not your own intention. CONTRAST with -겠지만: that is a drier 'probably... but,' while -ㄹ 텐데 leans warm and considerate, anticipating the listener's situation. Pitfall: English 'would' is ambiguous; here it is conjecture about a likely state, so don't use it for plans or promises.
commonMistakes: Confusing it with -ㄹ 건데 (a plan: 'I'm going to, but') — 내일 비가 올 텐데 is a GUESS about the weather, while 내일 갈 건데 is YOUR intention to go. Mixing them flips a forecast into a plan.
Using it for a fact you already know for certain — if you've confirmed they arrived, say 도착했는데, not 도착했을 텐데; 텐데 is specifically for an unconfirmed conjecture.
Forgetting the past form for a past guess — 'you must have been tired yesterday' is 어제 피곤했을 텐데, not 어제 피곤할 텐데, which would point the guess at the wrong time.

entries.english: (I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)
entries.shortExplanation: V-더니 means "(I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "(I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)" uses the pattern V-더니 (-deoni). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 그러더니 ("and then (after doing that)"). Attach -더니 directly to a verb or adjective stem (그러다 → 그러더니, 아프다 → 아프더니, 기침하다 → 기침하더니). The 더 is the 'I personally witnessed it' retrospective marker, so -더니 links something you SAW/HEARD firsthand in the past to the result or change that followed — 'he kept coughing (I watched it), and then he got sick.' The subject of plain -더니 is normally someone/something OTHER than 'I,' because you're reporting an outside observation. CONTRAST with -았/었더니: that combined form flips the subject to 'I' and means 'because I did/experienced X, this resulted' (많이 먹었더니 배불러 = I ate a lot, so now I'm full); use 었더니 for your own cause, plain 더니 for what you observed in others. CONTRAST with -니까: -니까 is a neutral logical 'because/since,' while -더니 always carries that eyewitness, watched-it-unfold flavor and a sense of change. Pitfall: don't narrate your own neutral actions with plain -더니 — it sounds odd to say 내가 가더니.

CONTRAST with -았/었더니: that combined form flips the subject to 'I' and means 'because I did/experienced X, this resulted' (많이 먹었더니 배불러 = I ate a lot, so now I'm full); use 었더니 for your own cause, plain 더니 for what you observed in others. commonMistakes: Using plain -더니 about your OWN action — for 'I overdid it, so...' say 내가 무리했더니, not 내가 무리하더니. Plain -더니 is for what you observed in someone/something else.

Mistaking -더니 for a neutral 'because' like -니까 — 비가 오니까 우산 챙겨 (since it's raining, take an umbrella) is logical reasoning, but 비가 오더니 길이 막히네 means 'it started raining and then, sure enough, the road jammed' — eyewitness change, not a request.

entries.english: since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)
entries.shortExplanation: V-길래 means "since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-길래 (-gillae) = "since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 싸길래 샀어요 ("it was cheap so I bought it"). Attach -길래 directly to a verb or adjective stem (싸다 → 싸길래, 울다 → 울길래, 맛있다 → 맛있길래); for nouns use N(이)길래. It gives a reason rooted in something you personally NOTICED or were told, which then prompted your own response — so the second clause is almost always YOUR own choice, usually past tense (싸길래 샀어요 = it was cheap, so I bought it). CONTRAST with -아서/어서: -아서 states a general or objective cause for any result (싸서 잘 팔려요 = it's cheap so it sells well, a fact about the world), but -길래 ties an observed reason specifically to what YOU then did in reaction. CONTRAST with -기에: same meaning, but -기에 is the more formal/written twin, while -길래 is conversational and warmer. Pitfall: the result clause cannot be a general truth or someone else's action — 'it's cheap so everyone buys it' is 싸서 다들 사요, not -길래; -길래 must lead to your own reactive deed. It also doesn't fit commands ('since it's cheap, buy it' uses 싸니까, not 싸길래).

entries.english: (it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 지 means "(it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ 지 (-(eu)n ji) means "(it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 온 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ("it hasn't been long since I came"). Add -ㄴ 지 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 온 지, 만나다 → 만난 지) and -은 지 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹은 지; 살다 drops ㄹ → 산 지). It measures the time ELAPSED since an action happened, and is normally followed by a duration plus 됐어요/지났어요 (한국에 온 지 1년 됐어요 = it's been a year since I came to Korea). Crucially, write 지 with a SPACE — this time-elapsed 지 is a separate noun-like word. CONTRAST sharply with the negative-ish -지 in 안/-지 않다: 온 지 1년 됐어요 (space; time since) vs 오지 않았어요 (no space; 'didn't come') are completely different 지. CONTRAST also with -(으)ㄴ 후에 'after': 온 후에 = once you've arrived (sequence), but 온 지 = how much time has passed since arriving (measurement) — they are not interchangeable. Pitfall: only works with verbs (an action that started the clock), never adjectives; ask elapsed time with 얼마나 됐어요? ('how long has it been?').

entries.english: the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ수록 means "the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ수록 (-(eu)l-surok). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 갈수록 ("more and more (as time goes on)"). Add -ㄹ수록 to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈수록, 보다 → 볼수록) and -을수록 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을수록; 알다 drops ㄹ → 알수록). It expresses proportional change: as one thing increases, another shifts along with it ('the more X, the more Y'). It is very commonly reinforced by putting -(으)면 on the front of the same verb — 보면 볼수록 (the more I look), 알면 알수록 (the more I learn) — a fixed, natural-sounding doubling. Write 수록 ATTACHED to the stem with no space. CONTRAST with -(으)니까/-아서 'because': those give a single cause→effect, but -ㄹ수록 sets up a sliding scale where Y keeps moving as X keeps growing. Pitfall: don't write a space (-ㄹ 수록 is wrong) and don't confuse it with the ability pattern -ㄹ 수 있다 — 갈수록 (more and more, one chunk) has nothing to do with 갈 수 있다 (can go). English 'the more... the more' uses two clauses with 'the'; Korean folds it into one suffix, so resist translating word for word.

entries.english: even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)
entries.shortExplanation: V-더라도 means "even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-더라도 (-deorado) = "even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 힘들더라도 ("even if it's hard"). Attach -더라도 directly to a verb or adjective stem (가다 → 가더라도, 힘들다 → 힘들더라도, 늦다 → 늦더라도); for nouns N(이)더라도. It concedes a strong or even unlikely hypothetical — 'even supposing that happens, the result still holds.' For a past supposition use -았/었더라도 (알았더라도 = even if I had known). It very often pairs with 아무리 ('no matter how') up front for extra force. CONTRAST with -아도/어도: both translate as 'even if,' but -아도 is the everyday, can-be-real concession (비가 와도 가요 = even if it rains I'll go, quite plausible), while -더라도 is stronger and more hypothetical, used for emphatic or less likely cases (비가 오더라도 = even supposing it rains). CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ/는데도 'even though,' which concedes a REAL current fact (비가 오는데도 = even though it IS raining), not a hypothetical. Pitfall: don't reach for -더라도 to describe something already happening — that's -는데도; reserve -더라도 for suppositions, especially after 아무리.

entries.nuance: Attach -더라도 directly to a verb or adjective stem (가다 → 가더라도, 힘들다 → 힘들더라도, 늦다 → 늦더라도); for nouns N(이)더라도. It concedes a strong or even unlikely hypothetical — 'even supposing that happens, the result still holds.' For a past supposition use -았/었더라도 (알았더라도 = even if I had known). It very often pairs with 아무리 ('no matter how') up front for extra force. CONTRAST with -아도/어도: both translate as 'even if,' but -아도 is the everyday, can-be-real concession (비가 와도 가요 = even if it rains I'll go, quite plausible), while -더라도 is stronger and more hypothetical, used for emphatic or less likely cases (비가 오더라도 = even supposing it rains). CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ/는데도 'even though,' which concedes a REAL current fact (비가 오는데도 = even though it IS raining), not a hypothetical. Pitfall: don't reach for -더라도 to describe something already happening — that's -는데도; reserve -더라도 for suppositions, especially after 아무리.

Forgetting the past form for a past hypothetical — 'even if I had known' is 알았더라도, not 알더라도, which would wrongly point the supposition at the present.

entries.english: have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 means "have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 (-(eu)l subakke eopda) means "have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 기다릴 수밖에 없어요 ("I have no choice but to wait"). Built from 수 ('way, possibility') + 밖에 ('except, outside of') + 없다 ('not exist'), so it literally says 'there is no way except doing it' — i.e. that one action is the sole remaining option, and you're resigned to it. Attach -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 to vowel stems (가다 → 갈 수밖에 없다), -을 수밖에 없다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 수밖에 없다); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 살 수밖에 없다). Past: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없었어요. CONTRAST: don't confuse it with the plain ability/possibility -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다. 갈 수 없어요 = 'I can't go (it's impossible)'; 갈 수밖에 없어요 = 'I have no choice but to go (going is the only option left).' The 밖에 flips the meaning from impossibility to inevitability. Note 밖에 always pairs with a negative (없다), and here it grammatically requires no 안 — 없다 already carries the negation. With adjectives it means 'is bound to be ~' (비싸다 → 비쌀 수밖에 없다 = it can't help but be expensive). PITFALL: English speakers reach for '~할 수 없다' when they mean 'I'm forced to'; that backfires into 'I cannot.' Also resist a space inside 수밖에.

entries.english: there's no way that / it can't possibly be that
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 means "there's no way that / it can't possibly be that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "there's no way that / it can't possibly be that" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 (-(eu)l riga eopda). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 그럴 리가 없어요 ("There's no way that's the case"). 리 here is the dependent noun 理 (Sino-Korean 'reason, principle'), so the phrase literally says 'there is no reason/grounds for it to be so' — a confident logical denial, not a wishy-washy guess. Attach -ㄹ 리가 없다 to vowel stems (오다 → 올 리가 없다), -을 리가 없다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 리가 없다). For a past doubt use -았/었을 리가 없다 (갔을 리가 없다 = no way they went); for nouns, N + 일 리가 없다 (사실 → 사실일 리가 없다). The 가 is routinely dropped in speech: -(으)ㄹ 리 없어요. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 vs -(으)ㄹ 리 만무하다 — both mean 'no way,' but 만무하다 (萬無, 'utterly absent') is bookish/written (올 리 만무하다 reads like an essay), while 리가 없다 is everyday spoken. Also distinguish it from the soft hedge -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 ('might'): 리가 없다 is the opposite pole — strong disbelief, 'surely not.' REGISTER: it carries emotional conviction (often surprise or indignation), so it lands naturally with -잖아/-는데. PITFALL: English speakers map 'there's no way' to time/possibility and grope for 방법(method) or 가능성(possibility); the idiomatic word is 리, and it must follow the -(으)ㄹ modifier, never stand alone.

entries.english: it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 means "it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 (-(eu)n/neun semida) = "it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 거의 다 한 셈이에요 ("It's basically all done"). 셈 is a native Korean noun meaning 'a count, a reckoning' (from 세다 'to count'), so this pattern frames a situation as 'when you tally it up, it effectively equals X' — reality isn't literally X, but practically counts as X. Present verbs take -는 셈이다 (사는 → 사는 셈이다), past/completed verbs -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (끝나다 → 끝난 셈이다), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (싸다 → 싼 셈이다). Often paired with 거의 ('almost') or 다 ('all'). CONTRAST: -는 셈이다 vs -(으)ㄴ/는 셈 치다 — 셈이다 states a calculated fact ('it amounts to ~'), whereas 셈 치다 means 'let's pretend/treat it as' a deliberate choice to regard something a certain way (속은 셈 치자 = 'let's just consider ourselves cheated and move on'). Also distinguish from -나 마나 (next door in this set): 셈이다 says 'it practically counts AS done,' not 'doing it is pointless.' REGISTER: neutral, very common in casual reasoning and explanations. PITFALL: English 'basically' is also a filler; here 셈이다 is a genuine equivalence claim, so don't tack it on to a literally-true statement (다 한 셈이에요 = 'practically done,' NOT '100% finished'). Match the modifier to tense — 끝난 셈 for a finished thing, not 끝나는 셈.

entries.english: might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 means "might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 (-(eu)ljido moreuda) means "might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 비 올지도 몰라요 ("It might rain"). Composed of the indirect-question modifier -(으)ㄹ지 ('whether ~') + 도 ('even') + 모르다 ('not know'), so it literally means 'I don't even know whether it'll happen' = there's a genuine chance. Attach -ㄹ지도 모르다 to vowel stems (오다 → 올지도 모르다), -을지도 모르다 to consonant stems (늦다 → 늦을지도 모르다). Past possibility: -았/었을지도 몰라요 (갔을지도 몰라요 = might have gone). 도 can drop for a slightly firmer hunch: -(으)ㄹ지 몰라요. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 vs -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 — both render 'might/probably,' but -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is an impression from evidence ('looks like it will,' 비 올 것 같아요 watching dark clouds), while -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 flags an uncertain possibility you want the listener to brace for ('it might rain, just so you know'). It also sits opposite -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 in this set: 리가 없다 = strong denial, -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 = open uncertainty. REGISTER: neutral; frequently used to soften warnings or hedge plans. PITFALL: 모르다 normally means 'don't know,' so beginners read 올지도 몰라요 as 'I don't know if it comes' — but as a fixed pattern it means 'might come.' Keep the -(으)ㄹ지 modifier intact; -는지/-(으)ㄴ지 would shift the time reference.

entries.english: is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)
entries.shortExplanation: V-기 마련이다 means "is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)" uses the pattern V-기 마련이다 (-gi maryeonida). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 사람은 누구나 실수하기 마련이에요 ("Everyone is bound to make mistakes"). 마련 is a native noun meaning 'a settled arrangement / the way things are set up,' so '-기 마련이다' states that an outcome is built into the nature of things — it's bound to happen, by default. Attach -기 마련이다 straight to any verb or adjective stem with no sound change (늙다 → 늙기 마련이다, 바쁘다 → 바쁘기 마련이다, 실수하다 → 실수하기 마련이다); nouns take N(이)기 마련이다. A fully synonymous variant is -게 마련이다 (실수하게 마련이다) — same meaning, freely interchangeable. CONTRAST: -기 마련이다 vs -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 — both touch 'inevitability,' but 마련이다 is a calm general truth about how the world tends to work ('people are bound to age'), while 수밖에 없다 is one person's forced choice in a specific situation ('I had no choice but to take a taxi'). REGISTER: neutral-to-reflective, the voice of proverbs and life lessons; it carries a soothing, philosophical tone, great for reassuring someone. PITFALL: English speakers borrow 'I'm bound to be late today' and try 마련이다 for a one-off — wrong; it's strictly for repeating, general truths, not a single scheduled event. Also attach to the bare stem, never the present modifier (실수하기/실수하게 마련, never 실수하는 마련).

entries.english: no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)나 마나 means "no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)나 마나 (-(eu)na mana) = "no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 보나 마나 뻔해요 ("It's obvious without even looking"). This sets the connective -(으)나 ('whether one does') against 마나 (a contracted -(으)나 of 말다, 'to not do'), so it weighs 'doing it' against 'not doing it' and concludes the two come out identical — hence 'no point.' Attach -나 마나 to vowel/ㄹ stems (보다 → 보나 마나) and -으나 마나 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹으나 마나); ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ (살다 → 사나 마나). It very often freezes into the adverb 보나 마나 = 'obviously, clearly (no need to even look).' CONTRAST: -(으)나 마나 vs -든지 말든지 — both involve 'do or don't,' but -(으)나 마나 means 'the outcome is the same, so it's futile' (your speaker's verdict), while -든지 말든지 means 'do it or not, I don't care / it's up to you' (indifference/leaving it to the other). Saying 가나 마나 = 'going won't change anything'; 가든지 말든지 = 'go or don't, whatever.' REGISTER: casual, slightly blunt — it dismisses the action as pointless, so use it among friends, not when politely deferring to a superior. PITFALL #1: 마나 comes from 말다, so never write 마라/말아 here. PITFALL #2: it's verb-only — you cannot say an adjective like 예쁘나 마나.

entries.english: half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)
entries.shortExplanation: V-는 둥 마는 둥 means "half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 둥 마는 둥 (-neun dung maneun dung) means "half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 했어요 ("I barely picked at my food"). 둥 is a dependent noun meaning roughly 'in such a manner,' and the pattern juxtaposes 'doing (-는 둥)' with 'not doing (마는 둥, from 말다),' painting an action performed so half-heartedly it's barely happening — distracted, rushed, going through the motions. Attach -는 둥 마는 둥 to a verb stem (먹다 → 먹는 둥 마는 둥, 듣다 → 듣는 둥 마는 둥); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 노는 둥 마는 둥). It's usually capped with 하다 or another verb describing what you did instead. CONTRAST: -는 둥 마는 둥 vs -(으)나 마나 — they look like cousins (both pair a verb with 말다) but mean opposite things. -는 둥 마는 둥 describes HOW you did it (sloppily, half-done — 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 = 'picked at the food'); -(으)나 마나 judges that doing it is POINTLESS because the result won't change (먹으나 마나 = 'no point eating'). Don't swap them. REGISTER: casual and vivid, slightly critical — it usually conveys distraction or lack of sincerity, so it's for describing behavior you found half-baked. PITFALL: the modifier of 말다 here is 마는 (the ㄹ drops before -는), so never write 말는. And it always takes present -는 둥; 먹은 둥 마는 둥 is wrong for this 'half-heartedly' meaning.
