entries.english: also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 겸 means "also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 겸 (-(eu)l gyeom). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 바람도 쐴 겸 산책해요 ("I take a walk partly to get some air"). 겸 is the Sino-Korean dependent noun 兼 ('combine, hold concurrently'), so -(으)ㄹ 겸 frames one action as serving two aims at once — 'partly in order to ~ (and partly for something else).' Attach -ㄹ 겸 to vowel stems (보다 → 볼 겸), -을 겸 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 겸); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 놀 겸). It very often comes doubled: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 ('partly to A, partly to B'), and a main action follows. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ 겸 vs -(으)러 (purpose 'in order to') — -(으)러 names the single main reason for going/coming (밥 먹으러 가다 = 'go in order to eat'), while -(으)ㄹ 겸 adds a SECONDARY purpose riding along ('while I'm at it, also to ~'), implying there's already another reason. So 산책할 겸 나왔어요 = 'I came out, and a walk was one of the reasons too.' REGISTER: neutral, everyday; great for casually justifying outings and two-birds-one-stone plans. PITFALL #1: use the future modifier -(으)ㄹ, never -는 겸 (볼 겸, not 보는 겸). PITFALL #2: 겸 cannot end a sentence by itself like a finite verb — it needs a following main action (볼 겸 왔어요), so don't stop at 볼 겸이에요.

entries.nuance: 겸 is the Sino-Korean dependent noun 兼 ('combine, hold concurrently'), so -(으)ㄹ 겸 frames one action as serving two aims at once — 'partly in order to ~ (and partly for something else).' Attach -ㄹ 겸 to vowel stems (보다 → 볼 겸), -을 겸 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 겸); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 놀 겸). It very often comes doubled: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 ('partly to A, partly to B'), and a main action follows. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ 겸 vs -(으)러 (purpose 'in order to') — -(으)러 names the single main reason for going/coming (밥 먹으러 가다 = 'go in order to eat'), while -(으)ㄹ 겸 adds a SECONDARY purpose riding along ('while I'm at it, also to ~'), implying there's already another reason. So 산책할 겸 나왔어요 = 'I came out, and a walk was one of the reasons too.' REGISTER: neutral, everyday; great for casually justifying outings and two-birds-one-stone plans. PITFALL #1: use the future modifier -(으)ㄹ, never -는 겸 (볼 겸, not 보는 겸). PITFALL #2: 겸 cannot end a sentence by itself like a finite verb — it needs a following main action (볼 겸 왔어요), so don't stop at 볼 겸이에요.
commonMistakes: Using the present modifier 보는 겸 — it's the future modifier -(으)ㄹ + 겸 (볼 겸).
Ending the sentence on 겸 (볼 겸이에요) — 겸 demands a following main action, e.g. 볼 겸 왔어요.
Substituting -(으)러 when there are two reasons. -(으)러 gives the single main purpose (보러 가다); -(으)ㄹ 겸 adds a side purpose to an action you'd do anyway.
Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

entries.english: tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)
entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 means "tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 (-(eu)n/neun pyeonida) = "tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 저는 매운 거 잘 먹는 편이에요 ("I'm on the side of handling spicy food well"). 편 is the Sino-Korean noun 便 ('side, group, leaning'), so '-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다' literally places something 'on the ~ side,' softening a claim from 'very' to 'rather/relatively.' Verbs take -는 편이다 (먹다 → 먹는 편이다), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 편이다 (크다 → 큰 편이다, 작다 → 작은 편이다); past habits use -(으)ㄴ 편이었다. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 vs the bare adjective — 키가 커요 asserts 'I am tall' flatly, while 키가 큰 편이에요 hedges to 'I'm on the taller side,' relative to others, sounding modest and non-absolute. It also differs from -(으)ㄴ/는 척하다 ('pretend to be') despite both using a 편/척 + 이다/하다 frame — 편이다 is an honest mild judgment, not a pretense. REGISTER: neutral and very polite-friendly; Koreans use it constantly for self-description and comparisons to avoid sounding boastful or blunt (술은 약한 편이에요 is gentler than 술 못 마셔요). PITFALL #1: match the modifier to word type — verbs -는 편 (먹는 편), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 편 (큰 편), so never 크는 편. PITFALL #2: because it means 'relatively,' don't pair it with intensifiers like 아주/완전 ('totally'); that contradicts the very softening it provides.

entries.english: do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)
entries.shortExplanation: V-기는 하다 means "do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-기는 하다 (-gineun hada) means "do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 먹기는 했어요 ("I did eat it (but...)"). Built from the nominalizer -기 + the contrast topic particle 는 + a dummy 하다 that echoes the verb's meaning, so it isolates and concedes one point ('as for doing it, yes') while signaling a 'but' is coming. Attach -기는 하다 to a verb or adjective stem (먹다 → 먹기는 하다, 좋다 → 좋기는 하다); in speech 기는 almost always contracts to 긴 (먹긴 해요). For tense, conjugate the final 하다 (먹기는 했어요 = 'I did eat, but...'); you can also fully repeat the verb instead of using 하다 (가긴 가다, 좋긴 좋다). CONTRAST: -기는 하다 vs -지만 — both pivot to a contrast, but -지만 is a neutral 'but' joining two clauses (좋지만 비싸요 = 'it's good but expensive'), whereas -기는 하다 first GRANTS/concedes the point with extra emphasis ('it IS good, I'll give you that... but'), carrying a reluctant, qualifying tone. So 좋긴 한데 비싸요 admits the merit before pushing back. It's usually followed by 그런데/근데 or -지만/-(으)ㄴ데. REGISTER: conversational and very common for soft disagreement, polite hedging, or a gentle 'no.' PITFALL: don't drop the verb's meaning into a bare 하다 — 가긴 하다 keeps 'go' via the repeated stem (or you say 가긴 가다); 가는 하다 is wrong. And since it sets up a contrast, 좋긴 해요 left alone feels unfinished unless the 'but' is understood.

entries.nuance: Built from the nominalizer -기 + the contrast topic particle 는 + a dummy 하다 that echoes the verb's meaning, so it isolates and concedes one point ('as for doing it, yes') while signaling a 'but' is coming. Attach -기는 하다 to a verb or adjective stem (먹다 → 먹기는 하다, 좋다 → 좋기는 하다); in speech 기는 almost always contracts to 긴 (먹긴 해요). For tense, conjugate the final 하다 (먹기는 했어요 = 'I did eat, but...'); you can also fully repeat the verb instead of using 하다 (가긴 가다, 좋긴 좋다). CONTRAST: -기는 하다 vs -지만 — both pivot to a contrast, but -지만 is a neutral 'but' joining two clauses (좋지만 비싸요 = 'it's good but expensive'), whereas -기는 하다 first GRANTS/concedes the point with extra emphasis ('it IS good, I'll give you that... but'), carrying a reluctant, qualifying tone. So 좋긴 한데 비싸요 admits the merit before pushing back. It's usually followed by 그런데/근데 or -지만/-(으)ㄴ데. REGISTER: conversational and very common for soft disagreement, polite hedging, or a gentle 'no.' PITFALL: don't drop the verb's meaning into a bare 하다 — 가긴 하다 keeps 'go' via the repeated stem (or you say 가긴 가다); 가는 하다 is wrong. And since it sets up a contrast, 좋긴 해요 left alone feels unfinished unless the 'but' is understood.
commonMistakes: Collapsing the verb into a bare 하다 (가는 하다) — you must repeat the action's meaning: 가긴 하다, or fully 가긴 가다.
Leaving it hanging without the contrast. It exists to set up a 'but,' so 좋긴 해요 by itself feels incomplete unless the qualifier is clearly implied.
Reaching for plain -지만 when you want to first concede with emphasis. -지만 is a neutral 'but'; -기는 하다 grants the point ('it IS good, granted...') before pushing back.

entries.shortExplanation: N을/를 좋아해요 means "to like N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "to like N" uses the pattern N을/를 좋아해요 (N-eul/reul joahaeyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 김치를 좋아해요 ("I like kimchi."). 좋아하다 is the VERB 'to like (something)', so the thing you like takes the object marker 을/를, not the subject marker 이/가. Add 을 after a consonant (음악을), 를 after a vowel (커피를). The huge English-speaker trap is its adjective cousin 좋다, which means 'is good/likeable' and takes 이/가: 커피가 좋아요 literally says 'coffee is good (to me)', while 커피를 좋아해요 says 'I like coffee' as an action with you as the doer — both translate to English 'I like coffee', but mixing the particles (커피가 좋아해요) is wrong. 좋아하다 conjugates as a regular 하다-style verb: stem 좋아하 + 여요 contracts to 좋아해요 in the 요-form, 좋아합니다 in formal speech. For people, 좋아하다 carries a romantic 'have a crush on' tone (그 사람을 좋아해요 = I have feelings for that person), so to say you merely enjoy someone's company use a softer phrasing. It pairs naturally with hobbies, food, music, and seasons.

entries.english: to go by N / toward N
entries.shortExplanation: N(으)로 가요 means "to go by N / toward N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N(으)로 가요 (N-(eu)ro gayo) = "to go by N / toward N". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 버스로 가요 ("I go by bus."). The particle (으)로 marks either the MEANS (by what / how) or the DIRECTION (toward which way) of a motion, so 버스로 가요 = 'go by bus' and 오른쪽으로 가요 = 'go to the right'. Attach 로 after a vowel or after the consonant ㄹ (지하철로, 서울로, 사무실로 — 사무실 ends in ㄹ), and 으로 after every other consonant (집으로, 부엌으로). The key contrast for English speakers is 에 vs (으)로: 에 marks a fixed DESTINATION you arrive at (서울에 가요 = go to Seoul, full stop), while (으)로 stresses the ROUTE or HEADING ('toward/in the direction of Seoul', not necessarily stopping there). For transport, English 'by bus' must become 버스로, never 버스에 — 버스에 가요 would weirdly mean 'go onto the bus'. With direction nouns (왼쪽, 이쪽, 위), only (으)로 works. It also collocates with 갈아타다 (지하철로 갈아타요 = transfer to the subway) and means/material more broadly (한국어로 말해요 = speak in Korean).

entries.english: to go in order to V
entries.shortExplanation: V(으)러 가요 means "to go in order to V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)러 가요 (V-(eu)reo gayo) means "to go in order to V" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥 먹으러 가요 ("I go to eat."). (으)러 attaches to a verb stem to state the PURPOSE of moving, and it is locked to motion verbs only — 가다, 오다, 다니다, 나가다 and the like. Add 러 to a vowel stem (만나러), 으러 to a consonant stem (먹으러); ㄹ stems keep the ㄹ and take 러 (놀러 가요 = go to hang out). The classic English-speaker confusion is (으)러 vs (으)려고: both mean 'in order to', but (으)러 must end in a going/coming verb and names only the errand of that trip (밥 먹으러 가요), whereas (으)려고 works with ANY main verb and expresses broader intention (밥 먹으려고 일찍 왔어요 = 'I came early intending to eat'). Word order matters: the place comes first with 에, then the purpose, then the motion verb — 도서관에 공부하러 가요, not '공부하러 도서관에 가요'-style English ordering. It frequently pairs with everyday errands: 사러(go to buy), 만나러(go to meet), 보러(go to watch a movie), 배우러(go to learn).

entries.shortExplanation: V아/어 보세요 means "try doing V (please)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "try doing V (please)" uses the pattern V아/어 보세요 (V-a/eo boseyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 먹어 보세요 ("Please try eating it."). V아/어 보다 means 'do V and see / give V a try', and in the imperative 보세요 it becomes a warm, polite suggestion — exactly what a shopkeeper, host, or friend says when recommending. Build the 아/어 form first: 아 after a stem vowel ㅏ or ㅗ (가 → 가 봐요), 어 otherwise (먹어 봐요), and 해 for 하다 verbs (해 보세요). The biggest pitfall is treating it as a literal command 'try!': it is softer and more inviting than the bare imperative 드세요/가세요, so 먹어 보세요 = 'why don't you give it a taste' rather than a blunt order. Don't confuse the suggestion 보세요 with the past 봤어요, which reports EXPERIENCE ('have you tried/done it before?': 한국 음식 먹어 봤어요?). Note also the homophone trap: 보다 here is the auxiliary 'try', not the main verb 'see/look'. It collocates with food (먹어/마셔 보세요), clothes (입어/신어 보세요), and gentle encouragement (한번 해 보세요 = give it a shot).

entries.shortExplanation: A-ㄴ/은 N means "an adjective describing a noun" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A-ㄴ/은 N (A-n/eun N) = "an adjective describing a noun". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 예쁜 가방 ("a pretty bag"). This is how a Korean ADJECTIVE attaches to a noun in front of it (the modifier always precedes the noun). Add ㄴ to a vowel stem (예쁘다 → 예쁜 가방) and 은 to a consonant stem (작다 → 작은 집); irregulars shift: ㅂ-adjectives like 춥다 become 추운 날씨, ㄹ stems drop ㄹ (길다 → 긴 머리). A core English-speaker trap is that 있다/없다-type 'adjectives' (맛있다, 재미없다) use the VERB-style ending 는, not 은: it's 맛있는 음식, never '맛있은'. Another is mixing this adjective-modifier with the verb-modifier: descriptive states take A-ㄴ/은 (작은 = 'small'), but ongoing actions take V-는 (먹는 = 'eating'). Don't carry over English word order — Korean never says 'a bag pretty'; the adjective sits before the noun with no copula. These modifiers pile up naturally: 작고 예쁜 집 ('a small, pretty house').

A core English-speaker trap is that 있다/없다-type 'adjectives' (맛있다, 재미없다) use the VERB-style ending 는, not 은: it's 맛있는 음식, never '맛있은'. Another is mixing this adjective-modifier with the verb-modifier: descriptive states take A-ㄴ/은 (작은 = 'small'), but ongoing actions take V-는 (먹는 = 'eating'). Don't carry over English word order — Korean never says 'a bag pretty'; the adjective sits before the noun with no copula. These modifiers pile up naturally: 작고 예쁜 집 ('a small, pretty house').

entries.english: a noun that does the verb
entries.shortExplanation: V-는 N means "a noun that does the verb" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-는 N (V-neun N) means "a noun that does the verb" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 먹는 사람 ("a person who eats"). Attach 는 to a verb stem to turn the verb into a present-tense modifier describing the noun behind it: 먹는 사람 = 'a person who is eating / who eats'. This is Korean's equivalent of an English relative clause ('the person WHO eats'), but it sits in FRONT of the noun, so the whole clause is read right-to-left into English. ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ before 는: 살다 → 사는 곳 ('the place where I live'), 알다 → 아는 사람 ('someone I know'). The key tense contrast English speakers must learn: V-는 = present/habitual action (가는 버스 = 'the bus that goes'), V-(으)ㄴ = completed/past (간 사람 = 'the person who went'), V-(으)ㄹ = future/prospective (갈 사람 = 'the person who will go'). Don't confuse this verb 는 with the adjective modifier A-ㄴ/은; only 있다/없다 adjectives borrow the 는 form. Common partners: 사는 곳, 아는 사람, 좋아하는 음식, 자주 가는 가게.

entries.english: it seems like N / looks like N
entries.shortExplanation: N 같아요 means "it seems like N / looks like N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "it seems like N / looks like N" uses the pattern N 같아요 (N gatayo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 학생 같아요 ("He seems like a student."). N 같다 means 'is like N / seems to be N', expressing a resemblance or a soft guess, and the noun sits directly before 같아요 with NO object or subject marker (학생 같아요, never '학생을 같아요'). The adjective 같다 conjugates as a regular ㅏ-stem: 같 + 아요 → 같아요. Two contrasts matter for English speakers. First, 같다 ('same/like') vs 비슷하다 ('similar'): 같다 leans toward 'practically identical / seems to BE it' (쌍둥이 같아요 = 'they're like twins'), while 비슷하다 just means 'roughly alike'. Second, this NOUN-pattern (N 같아요) is a guess about identity or likeness, whereas the VERB/ADJECTIVE pattern V/A-(으)ㄴ/는 것 같아요 expresses a tentative judgment about a situation (비가 오는 것 같아요 = 'it seems to be raining'). A frequent trap is forcing 처럼 here: 처럼 ('like, as') modifies a following verb (천사처럼 웃어요 = 'smiles like an angel'), but to predicate 'it seems like an angel' you need 천사 같아요. Collocates with impressions: 꿈 같아요, 거짓말 같아요, 진짜 같아요.

entries.shortExplanation: N보다 더 A means "more A than N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N보다 더 A (N-boda deo A) = "more A than N". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 저보다 더 커요 ("taller than me"). 보다 is the comparison particle 'than', and it attaches to the STANDARD you measure against (the thing being beaten), then 더 ('more') plus the adjective: 저보다 더 커요 = 'taller than me'. A frequent English-speaker error is attaching 보다 to the wrong side — in '오늘은 어제보다 더 추워요', the topic 오늘 is what's colder and 어제 (yesterday) is the baseline with 보다, mirroring English 'today is colder THAN yesterday'. 더 is often optional and idiomatic (어제보다 추워요 already implies 'colder'), but adding 더 sounds natural and emphatic; its opposite 덜 means 'less' (어제보다 덜 추워요 = 'less cold than yesterday'). For the superlative 'the most', switch to 제일/가장 (제일 커요 = 'the biggest'). Don't use 보다 with a 'than' clause the English way before a verb — Korean keeps it as 'N보다'. It collocates with size, speed, weather, and quantity: 키가 커요, 빨라요, 더워요, 많아요.

entries.shortExplanation: V기로 했어요 means "decided to V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V기로 했어요 (V-giro haesseoyo) means "decided to V" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 가기로 했어요 ("I decided to go."). V기로 하다 reports a DECISION or resolution to do something; 기 nominalizes the verb, 로 marks it as the chosen course, and 하다 ('to do/decide') is kept in the past 했어요 because the deciding already happened — even when the action itself is future (내일 가기로 했어요 = 'I('ve) decided to go tomorrow'). Attach 기로 했어요 straight to the plain stem (가기로, 배우기로, 운동하기로); for the negative, put 안 before the verb (안 먹기로 했어요 = 'decided not to eat'). The main English-speaker pitfall is conjugating 하다 to the future (가기로 할 거예요 is a different nuance: 'I'm going to decide') or to the present (가기로 해요 sounds like a soft proposal 'let's decide to go'); for an already-settled plan, lock it in the past: 했어요. Contrast with V(으)ㄹ게요, which is an on-the-spot promise/volition ('I'll do it', 제가 갈게요), whereas 기로 했어요 reports a decision reached beforehand, often a mutual or deliberate one. It collocates with resolutions and arrangements: 같이 가기로 했어요, 끊기로 했어요, 매일 운동하기로 했어요.

entries.shortExplanation: N 동안 means "during N / for N (duration)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "during N / for N (duration)" uses the pattern N 동안 (N dongan). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 한 시간 동안 ("for one hour"). 동안 is a duration noun meaning 'the span / while', placed after a time-length noun to say how long something lasts: 한 시간 동안 = 'for one hour', 방학 동안 = 'during the vacation'. No particle goes between the noun and 동안 (한 시간 동안, never '한 시간에 동안'). The crucial English-speaker contrast is 동안 vs 에: 에 pins an action to a POINT in time ('AT 3 o'clock', 세 시에 갔어요), while 동안 stretches it over a STRETCH of time ('FOR three hours'). So 'I studied for three hours' is 세 시간 동안 공부했어요, but 'I studied at three' is 세 시에 공부했어요. With a verb clause it becomes V-는 동안 ('while ~ing': 제가 자는 동안 = 'while I sleep'). Also distinguish 동안 (a duration) from 까지 (a deadline 'until'): 'until 3' is 세 시까지, 'for 3 hours' is 세 시간 동안 — English 'for' here is NOT 위해(서). It collocates with study, travel, waiting, and stays: 공부했어요, 여행했어요, 기다렸어요, 살았어요.

entries.english: intend to V / plan to V
entries.shortExplanation: V(으)려고 해요 means "intend to V / plan to V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)려고 해요 (V-(eu)ryeogo haeyo) = "intend to V / plan to V". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 가려고 해요 ("I plan to go."). Use this to announce your own intention or a not-yet-fixed plan: the verb 하다 at the end literally means you are 'trying to / setting out to' do the verb. Form it by adding 려고 after a vowel stem (가다 -> 가려고 해요) and 으려고 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹으려고 해요), then attach 해요. Sharp contrast: -(으)려고 해요 is a leaning or wish, softer and less committed than -(으)ㄹ 거예요, which is a settled decision; '내일 자려고 해요' = 'I'm thinking of sleeping early' whereas '내일 잘 거예요' = 'I will sleep early.' English-speaker pitfall: this is for the speaker's mind, so do not use it to report what someone else firmly will do, and never bolt a noun onto it — say '공부하려고 해요', not '공부 하려고 해요'.

entries.shortExplanation: V아/어 주시겠어요? means "could you please V?" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V아/어 주시겠어요? (V-a/eo jusigesseoyo) means "could you please V?" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 도와주시겠어요? ("Could you please help me?"). This is the gentlest everyday way to ask a favor of someone you don't know well: 주다 ('do it for me') becomes honorific 주시다, and the -겠- adds a tentative 'would you mind' softness that a flat 주세요 lacks. Build the 아/어 form (도와 from 돕다, 열어 from 열다, 말해 from 말하다), then add 주시겠어요. Contrast: 주세요 is a clear polite request ('please do X'), while 주시겠어요? is a deferential question ('might I ask you to X?') — perfect for staff, strangers, or anyone senior; 줄래? in the casual tab is only for close friends. Pitfall: English speakers often forget the 아/어 link and say '돕아 주시겠어요' — the verb 돕다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it must be 도와 주시겠어요.

entries.english: it is good to V / you should V
entries.shortExplanation: V는 게 좋아요 means "it is good to V / you should V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "it is good to V / you should V" uses the pattern V는 게 좋아요 (V-neun ge joayo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 가는 게 좋아요 ("It's good to go."). This gives gentle, non-pushy advice — literally 'doing V is good' — so it lands much softer than a direct order. Attach 는 게 좋아요 to the dictionary stem (가다 -> 가는 게 좋아요); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 는, so 만들다 -> 만드는 게 좋아요 and 살다 -> 사는 게 좋아요. The 게 here is a contraction of 것이 ('the thing of doing X'). Sharp contrast: 는 게 좋아요 is a friendly recommendation, whereas -아/어야 해요 is an obligation you cannot skip; '쉬는 게 좋아요' = 'you'd be better off resting' but '쉬어야 해요' = 'you have to rest.' Pitfall: don't write the past 'V은 게 좋아요' for advice — advice about an action you should take always uses the present 는 게, since you're recommending it now.

entries.english: I think it will / it seems
entries.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 means "I think it will / it seems" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 (A/V-(eu)l geot gatayo) = "I think it will / it seems". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 비가 올 것 같아요 ("I think it'll rain."). Use this to make a soft prediction or guess about something not yet certain — literally 'it seems like the thing that will happen.' Add ㄹ 것 같아요 after a vowel stem (오다 -> 올 것 같아요) and 을 것 같아요 after a consonant stem (늦다 -> 늦을 것 같아요); 같다 means 'to be like / seem.' Important contrast inside this same pattern: the -(으)ㄹ form is a guess about the future or the uncertain ('비가 올 것 같아요' = 'it looks like it'll rain'), while -는 것 같아요 guesses about right now ('비가 오는 것 같아요' = 'it seems to be raining') and -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 guesses about the past ('비가 온 것 같아요' = 'it seems it rained'). Pitfall: English 'I think' is often a firm opinion, but -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is deliberately tentative and polite, so don't use it when you actually know — for certainty use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

entries.shortExplanation: V(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 means "have done V before" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 (V-(eu)n jeogi isseoyo) means "have done V before" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 가 본 적이 있어요 ("I've been there before."). This is the 'have you ever...' experience pattern: 적 is a bound noun meaning 'a (past) occasion,' so the whole thing literally says 'there exists an occasion on which I did V.' Add ㄴ 적이 있어요 after a vowel stem (가다 -> 간 적이 있어요) and 은 적이 있어요 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹은 적이 있어요); swap 있어요 for 없어요 to say you never have. Sharp contrast with plain past tense: -았/었어요 just reports that something happened ('어제 갔어요' = 'I went yesterday'), while -(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 highlights it as a life experience worth noting ('가 본 적이 있어요' = 'I've had the experience of going'), so it pairs naturally with -아/어 보다 ('try'). Pitfall: don't use it for a recent or one-time event you'd describe with a date — 'I ate breakfast this morning' is 아침을 먹었어요, not 먹은 적이 있어요.

entries.shortExplanation: N 때문에 means "because of N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "because of N" uses the pattern N 때문에 (N ttaemune). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 비 때문에 ("because of the rain"). Use this to name a noun as the cause of something, usually a result you didn't choose — it leans toward blame or unwanted consequences. Place the noun directly before 때문에 with no particle (비 때문에, 일 때문에). Sharp contrast: 때문에 most often introduces a negative cause ('비 때문에 취소했어요' = 'I canceled because of the rain'), whereas 덕분에 ('thanks to') introduces a positive cause you're grateful for ('친구 덕분에 잘 끝났어요'), so swapping them changes the whole tone. Also note 때문에 takes a NOUN; to give a verb/adjective reason you must say -기 때문에 (바쁘기 때문에). Pitfall: English 'because' is one word that handles both, but Korean splits noun-cause (때문에) from clause-cause (-아서 / -니까 / -기 때문에), and learners wrongly insert a particle — it's 비 때문에, never 비가 때문에.

entries.english: because / since V (reason for a request)
entries.shortExplanation: V(으)니까 means "because / since V (reason for a request)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)니까 (V-(eu)nikka) = "because / since V (reason for a request)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 비가 오니까 ("since it's raining"). This gives a reason that the speaker is presenting as grounds for what comes next — a request, a suggestion, or a command — so it's the 'since...' that leads into 'so let's / so please.' Add 니까 after a vowel stem (오다 -> 오니까) and 으니까 after a consonant stem (없다 -> 없으니까). Crucial contrast: -(으)니까 vs -아/어서. Use -니까 before an order, request, or suggestion ('비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요'), but -아/어서 before a plain statement of result and never before a command ('비가 와서 못 갔어요' = 'I couldn't go because it rained'). Also, -아/어서 cannot carry a past-tense marker on its clause, but -니까 can (갔으니까). Pitfall: English speakers default to one 'because' everywhere — saying '늦어서 미안해요' is right, but '늦으니까 미안해요' sounds like you're justifying yourself rather than apologizing, so for apologies and pure cause use -아/어서.

entries.nuance: This gives a reason that the speaker is presenting as grounds for what comes next — a request, a suggestion, or a command — so it's the 'since...' that leads into 'so let's / so please.' Add 니까 after a vowel stem (오다 -> 오니까) and 으니까 after a consonant stem (없다 -> 없으니까). Crucial contrast: -(으)니까 vs -아/어서. Use -니까 before an order, request, or suggestion ('비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요'), but -아/어서 before a plain statement of result and never before a command ('비가 와서 못 갔어요' = 'I couldn't go because it rained'). Also, -아/어서 cannot carry a past-tense marker on its clause, but -니까 can (갔으니까). Pitfall: English speakers default to one 'because' everywhere — saying '늦어서 미안해요' is right, but '늦으니까 미안해요' sounds like you're justifying yourself rather than apologizing, so for apologies and pure cause use -아/어서.

entries.shortExplanation: N처럼 means "like N / as N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N처럼 (N-cheoreom) means "like N / as N" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 가수처럼 ("like a singer"). Use this to say one thing resembles or behaves the same way as a noun — 'like / just as.' Attach 처럼 directly to the noun with no particle (가수처럼, 꿈처럼). Sharp contrast: 처럼 expresses likeness or equal degree ('가수처럼 노래해요' = 'sings like a singer'), but 보다 expresses inequality / comparison ('가수보다 잘해요' = 'sings better than a singer'), so they are opposites — one means 'similar to,' the other 'more/less than.' 처럼 also overlaps with 같이 in this sense (가수같이 노래해요 ≈ 가수처럼 노래해요), though 처럼 is the more neutral default. Pitfall: English 'like' doubles as 'such as' for examples, but Korean 처럼 only means 'resembling'; to list examples ('fruits like apples') you'd use 같은 (사과 같은 과일), not 사과처럼 과일.

entries.english: even if V / even though V
entries.shortExplanation: V아/어도 means "even if V / even though V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "even if V / even though V" uses the pattern V아/어도 (V-a/eodo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 비가 와도 ("even if it rains"). This concedes a condition that doesn't change the outcome — 'even if / even though.' Build the 아/어 form, then add 도 ('also/even'): use 아 after a bright vowel ㅏ or ㅗ (가다 -> 가도, 오다 -> 와도), 어 otherwise (먹다 -> 먹어도), and 해 for 하다 verbs (공부해도). Contrast with -(으)면 ('if'): -(으)면 says the result depends on the condition ('비가 오면 안 가요' = 'if it rains I won't go'), while -아/어도 says the result holds in spite of it ('비가 와도 가요' = 'even if it rains, I'll go') — so they point in opposite directions. It also overlaps with -지만 ('but'), but -아/어도 is hypothetical ('even if it were') whereas -지만 reports an actual fact ('비싸지만 샀어요' = 'it was expensive but I bought it'). Pitfall: pick the vowel by sound, not by spelling out the stem — 오다 contracts to 와도, never 오아도.

entries.english: while doing V (at the same time)
entries.shortExplanation: V(으)면서 means "while doing V (at the same time)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)면서 (V-(eu)myeonseo) = "while doing V (at the same time)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 걸으면서 ("while walking"). Use this when one person does two actions at the same moment — the action in the 면서 clause runs concurrently with the main verb. Add 면서 after a vowel stem (보다 -> 보면서) and 으면서 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹으면서); for ㄷ-irregular verbs the ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 -> 들으면서). Key rule and contrast: the subject of both actions must be the SAME person, which is exactly how -(으)면서 differs from -(으)ㄹ 때 ('when,' which just sets a time and allows different subjects) and from -고 ('and then,' which lets actions be sequential rather than overlapping). 'TV를 보면서 밥을 먹어요' = doing both at once; 'TV를 보고 밥을 먹어요' = watch first, then eat. Pitfall: English 'while' can cover two different people ('while I cooked, he cleaned'), but Korean -(으)면서 cannot — for two separate subjects acting at once use -는 동안 (동안 = 'during') instead.

entries.nuance: Use this when one person does two actions at the same moment — the action in the 면서 clause runs concurrently with the main verb. Add 면서 after a vowel stem (보다 -> 보면서) and 으면서 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹으면서); for ㄷ-irregular verbs the ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 -> 들으면서). Key rule and contrast: the subject of both actions must be the SAME person, which is exactly how -(으)면서 differs from -(으)ㄹ 때 ('when,' which just sets a time and allows different subjects) and from -고 ('and then,' which lets actions be sequential rather than overlapping). 'TV를 보면서 밥을 먹어요' = doing both at once; 'TV를 보고 밥을 먹어요' = watch first, then eat. Pitfall: English 'while' can cover two different people ('while I cooked, he cleaned'), but Korean -(으)면서 cannot — for two separate subjects acting at once use -는 동안 (동안 = 'during') instead.
commonMistakes: 제가 요리하면서 동생이 청소했어요.
면서 requires one shared subject; here 'I' and 'my sibling' differ, so it's ungrammatical.

듣으면서 공부해요.
듣다 is ㄷ-irregular, so before 으 the ㄷ changes to ㄹ.
Say 들으면서 공부해요.

entries.shortExplanation: V기 시작하다 means "start doing" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V기 시작하다 (-gi sijakada) means "start doing" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 저는 한국어를 배우기 시작했어요. ("I started learning Korean."). This pattern turns a verb into a noun with 기 and then feeds it to 시작하다 (始作하다, Sino-Korean 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do'), so literally you are 'doing the beginning of the action'. Use it when you want to spotlight the very moment an action gets underway: 비가 오기 시작했어요 ('it started to rain'). The close rival is plain 시작하다 with a noun object, 공부를 시작하다 ('start studying'): use that when the activity is already a noun, but use V기 시작하다 when you have a verb and want to keep its verb meaning. English speakers carry over 'start to' versus 'start -ing' as if Korean had two forms, but Korean only has this one, so do not say 오게 시작하다 or 와서 시작하다. The other trap is attaching 기 to a noun: 비기 시작하다 is wrong because 비 is already a noun; you need a verb stem like 오- before 기.

entries.shortExplanation: V게 되다 means "come to / end up" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "come to / end up" uses the pattern V게 되다 (-ge doeda). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 한국에 살게 됐어요. ("I ended up living in Korea."). V게 되다 frames a result as something that happened TO you rather than something you chose: 되다 means 'become', so the whole thing says 'it came to be that...'. Reach for it when outside circumstances, fate, or other people produced the outcome — 한국에 살게 됐어요 quietly signals 'it worked out that I live in Korea', softer and more humble than 한국에 살아요 ('I live in Korea', a flat fact). Contrast it sharply with V기로 하다, which marks a firm personal decision: 회사를 그만두기로 했어요 = 'I decided to quit' (my will), whereas 회사를 그만두게 됐어요 = 'I ended up quitting' (circumstances pushed me). Koreans love this pattern precisely because it downplays personal agency, which sounds modest and polite. The English-speaker pitfall is overusing it for plain decisions — if you clearly chose something, 게 되다 sounds evasive, as if you are dodging responsibility. Also note the spelling: 되다 contracts to 돼요 (되 + 어요), not 되요, in casual and polite speech.

entries.shortExplanation: V아/어 있다 means "state continues" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V아/어 있다 (-a/eo itda) = "state continues". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 문이 열려 있어요. ("The door is open."). V아/어 있다 describes the lingering STATE left behind after an action finishes: the door was opened and stays open, so 문이 열려 있어요 ('the door is open'). Pick 아 있다 when the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (앉아 있다) and 어 있다 otherwise (열려 있다, 서 있다). The notorious confusion is with V고 있다, the progressive: 고 있다 is the action still happening, 아/어 있다 is the result still in place. So 앉고 있어요 = 'I am (in the act of) sitting down', while 앉아 있어요 = 'I am seated'; 문을 열고 있어요 = 'I am opening the door', 문이 열려 있어요 = 'the door is (already) open'. Notice 아/어 있다 takes mostly intransitive or passive verbs (오다, 가다, 서다, 열리다, 켜지다) and the noun gets 이/가, not 을/를. The English-speaker trap is using it with transitive action verbs like 먹다 or 읽다: 밥을 먹어 있어요 is wrong; an action you keep doing needs 고 있다 (밥을 먹고 있어요).

entries.nuance: V아/어 있다 describes the lingering STATE left behind after an action finishes: the door was opened and stays open, so 문이 열려 있어요 ('the door is open'). Pick 아 있다 when the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (앉아 있다) and 어 있다 otherwise (열려 있다, 서 있다). The notorious confusion is with V고 있다, the progressive: 고 있다 is the action still happening, 아/어 있다 is the result still in place. So 앉고 있어요 = 'I am (in the act of) sitting down', while 앉아 있어요 = 'I am seated'; 문을 열고 있어요 = 'I am opening the door', 문이 열려 있어요 = 'the door is (already) open'. Notice 아/어 있다 takes mostly intransitive or passive verbs (오다, 가다, 서다, 열리다, 켜지다) and the noun gets 이/가, not 을/를. The English-speaker trap is using it with transitive action verbs like 먹다 or 읽다: 밥을 먹어 있어요 is wrong; an action you keep doing needs 고 있다 (밥을 먹고 있어요).
commonMistakes: Saying 밥을 먹어 있어요 for 'I am eating'. 먹다 is an ongoing action, not a resulting state, so it needs 고 있다: 밥을 먹고 있어요.
Marking the subject with 을/를, e.g. 문을 열려 있어요. With 아/어 있다 the thing is in a state, so it takes 이/가: 문이 열려 있어요.
Mixing up 앉고 있다 and 앉아 있다. 앉고 있다 = the act of sitting down in progress; 앉아 있다 = already seated. Learners often want the second meaning but say the first.

entries.shortExplanation: V(으)ㄹ 때 means "when" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)ㄹ 때 (-(eu)l ttae) means "when" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥을 먹을 때 물을 마셔요. ("When I eat, I drink water."). 때 is the noun 'time/occasion', so V(으)ㄹ 때 literally means 'the time when V', naming the moment an action or state holds: 밥을 먹을 때 = 'when (I) eat'. Attach ㄹ 때 after a vowel-final stem (갈 때) and 을 때 after a consonant-final stem (먹을 때, 좋을 때). This works with adjectives too — 피곤할 때 ('when tired') — which sets it apart from time markers reserved for verbs. The key contrast is with the connective -(으)면 ('if/whenever'): -(으)ㄹ 때 pins down a specific occasion or duration ('during the time when'), while -(으)면 states a condition ('if it happens'). So 비가 올 때 우산을 써요 = 'when it rains (at that time) I use an umbrella', whereas 비가 오면 = 'if/whenever it rains'. For a completed past moment, switch to V았/었을 때: 어렸을 때 ('when I was young'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the 으: consonant stems need it (좋을 때, not 좋ㄹ 때), and learners often forget that 때 is a real noun that can take particles like 에 or 부터.

entries.shortExplanation: V는 동안 means "while / during" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "while / during" uses the pattern V는 동안 (-neun dongan). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 제가 요리하는 동안 기다려 주세요. ("Please wait while I cook."). 동안 is the noun 'a stretch of time/duration', so V는 동안 means 'during the whole time that V is going on', framing two events that share the same span: 제가 요리하는 동안 기다려 주세요 ('please wait while I cook'). Because 동안 is a present-tense duration noun, the verb takes the 는 modifier ending, never 은. Contrast it with V(으)ㄹ 때: 때 points at the moment or occasion ('at the time when'), while 동안 stresses the continuous span throughout which something runs in parallel. So 자는 동안 = 'all the while I sleep (the whole duration)', whereas 잘 때 = 'when I sleep / at sleeping time'. 동안 can also stand alone after a plain noun of duration: 방학 동안 ('during the vacation'), 한 시간 동안 ('for one hour'). The English-speaker pitfall is attaching 은 instead of 는 (자은 동안 is wrong; it must be 자는 동안), and translating 'while' too loosely — if you mean contrast ('while X, Y is different'), Korean uses -는데 or -지만, not 동안, which is purely about overlapping time.

entries.shortExplanation: A/V-지만 means "but" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: A/V-지만 (-jiman) = "but". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 한국어는 어렵지만 재미있어요. ("Korean is hard but fun."). -지만 clips straight onto a verb or adjective stem to join two clauses that pull against each other: 한국어는 어렵지만 재미있어요 ('Korean is hard but fun'). It is the everyday, neutral 'but', equally at home in writing and speech. The sharp contrast to learn is -지만 versus -는데: -지만 states a clean, head-on opposition (A, but the opposite B), while -는데 gives softer background or contrast that sets up the next remark — 비싸지만 샀어요 simply says 'expensive but I bought it', whereas 비싼데 살까요? leans into 'it's pricey, so... should I buy it?'. After a noun you need the copula: 학생이지만 ('though I'm a student'), not 학생지만. Tense usually sits on the final clause, not before 지만, so 'I was tired but studied' is 피곤하지만 공부했어요, with 했 carrying the past. entries.shortExplanation: V거나 means "or" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V거나 (-geona) means "or" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 주말에 자거나 영화를 봐요. ("On weekends I sleep or watch movies."). -거나 attaches to a verb (or adjective) stem to offer alternative ACTIONS — 'do this or do that' — when either option is fine: 주말에 자거나 영화를 봐요 ('on weekends I sleep or watch a movie'). The crucial split for English speakers is that Korean splits 'or' by part of speech: -거나 joins verbs/adjectives, while (이)나 joins nouns. So 'coffee or tea' (two nouns) is 커피나 차, but 'drink coffee or drink tea' (two verbs) is 커피를 마시거나 차를 마셔요. A second rival is -든지, which adds a 'whichever, no matter which' nuance ('do whatever, sleep or watch a movie, I don't care'), while plain -거나 just lists open options neutrally. You can chain more than two: 자거나 먹거나 쉬어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using 거나 to connect nouns (커피거나 차 is wrong — use 커피나 차) and confusing it with 아니면 ('or else / otherwise'), which links whole sentences rather than gluing two verbs inside one clause.

entries.shortExplanation: N마다 means "every" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "every" uses the pattern N마다 (-mada). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 저는 아침마다 운동해요. ("I work out every morning."). 마다 is a particle you stick onto a noun to mean 'each / every one without exception', and it carries two flavors: with a time noun it means 'every time' (아침마다 = 'every morning'), and with a countable noun it means 'each individual one' (사람마다 = 'each person'). It often pairs with 다르다 to say things differ case by case: 나라마다 문화가 달라요 ('every country has a different culture'). Compare it with the standalone 매 (every) and 모든 (all): 매일 and 날마다 both mean 'every day', but 매 attaches to specific time words (매일, 매주, 매년) while 마다 is freer and can ride any noun (가게마다, 집집마다). And 모든 사람 ('all people') views the group as a whole, whereas 사람마다 zooms in on each member one by one. The English-speaker pitfall is attaching 마다 to a verb (자마다 is wrong) — for 'every time you do X' you need V(으)ㄹ 때마다 (잘 때마다) — and reaching for 매 with nouns it doesn't take, where 마다 is the safe, productive choice.

Compare it with the standalone 매 (every) and 모든 (all): 매일 and 날마다 both mean 'every day', but 매 attaches to specific time words (매일, 매주, 매년) while 마다 is freer and can ride any noun (가게마다, 집집마다). And 모든 사람 ('all people') views the group as a whole, whereas 사람마다 zooms in on each member one by one. The English-speaker pitfall is attaching 마다 to a verb (자마다 is wrong) — for 'every time you do X' you need V(으)ㄹ 때마다 (잘 때마다) — and reaching for 매 with nouns it doesn't take, where 마다 is the safe, productive choice.

entries.shortExplanation: V자마자 means "as soon as" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V자마자 (-jamaja) = "as soon as". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 집에 오자마자 손을 씻어요. ("The moment I get home, I wash my hands."). -자마자 fuses onto a verb stem to say the second action follows the first with zero gap: 집에 오자마자 손을 씻어요 ('the moment I get home, I wash my hands'). It is the tightest 'right after' connector. Compare it with V은/ㄴ 후에 ('after'), which only says B happens later, allowing any delay, while 자마자 insists on immediacy and often a touch of surprise — 도착한 후에 전화해요 = 'I'll call sometime after arriving', but 도착하자마자 전화해요 = 'I'll call the instant I arrive'. Two grammar facts trip learners up: never put a tense marker before 자마자 (write 끝나자마자, not 끝났자마자) even when the whole sentence is past, because the final verb carries the tense — 보자마자 웃었어요 ('I laughed the moment I saw it'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like 'as soon as' clauses that take their own tense in English ('as soon as I arrived'), and confusing it with the time noun phrase V는 대로, which is more formal and planning-oriented ('as soon as it's done, per arrangement').

entries.shortExplanation: V(으)려면 means "if you intend to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V(으)려면 (-(eu)ryeomyeon) means "if you intend to" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 한국어를 잘하려면 매일 연습해요. ("To get good at Korean, practice daily."). V(으)려면 is a contraction of 려고 하면 ('if you intend/plan to'), so it sets up a goal and then states what you must do to reach it: 한국어를 잘하려면 매일 연습해요 ('if you mean to get good at Korean, practice daily'). Use 려면 after a vowel-final stem (가려면, 잘하려면) and 으려면 after a consonant-final stem (읽으려면, 먹으려면). It naturally leads into advice or requirements, so it loves to pair with 야 하다/돼요, 세요, or 필요하다: 건강하려면 잘 자야 해요. Contrast it with the plain conditional -(으)면, which states a neutral 'if/when' about facts, while -(으)려면 specifically frames a deliberate goal or intention you are aiming at: 비가 오면 = 'if it rains' (a circumstance), but 살을 빼려면 = 'if you intend to lose weight' (your aim). The English-speaker pitfalls are dropping the 으 on consonant stems (읽려면 is wrong — say 읽으려면) and using 려면 for things outside your control; since it implies intention, you would not say 비가 오려면 for 'if it rains', because rain is not something you intend.

entries.shortExplanation: V았/었어요 means "polite past tense" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "polite past tense" uses the pattern V았/었어요 (Vat/eosseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 어제 밥을 먹었어요. ("I ate rice yesterday."). Take the verb stem. If the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요; all other vowels add 었어요. Contracted stems: 하다 → 했어요; 오다 → 왔어요; 보다 → 봤어요. Irregular ㅂ stems drop ㅂ and add 웠어요 (춥다 → 추웠어요). Irregular ㄷ stems change ㄷ to ㄹ before 었어요 (듣다 → 들었어요). Irregular ㅅ stems drop ㅅ (낫다 → 나았어요). Irregular 르 stems: 모르다 → 몰랐어요, 다르다 → 달랐어요. Contrast with V-고 있었어요 (past progressive) and V았/었었어요 (remote past / past-perfect nuance). The doubled past 았/었었어요 signals an action that was true in the past but is no longer true: 살았었어요 = 'I used to live there (but no longer do)'. Avoid confusing the ㅂ-irregular past 웠어요 with the future -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

Contrast with V-고 있었어요 (past progressive) and V았/었었어요 (remote past / past-perfect nuance). The doubled past 았/었었어요 signals an action that was true in the past but is no longer true: 살았었어요 = 'I used to live there (but no longer do)'. Avoid confusing the ㅂ-irregular past 웠어요 with the future -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

entries.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 means "future tense / strong intention" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 (V-(eu)r geoyeyo) = "future tense / strong intention". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 내일 친구를 만날 거예요. ("I will meet a friend tomorrow."). Take the verb stem. After a vowel-final stem add -ㄹ 거예요 (가다 → 갈 거예요, 하다 → 할 거예요). After a consonant-final stem add -을 거예요 (먹다 → 먹을 거예요, 읽다 → 읽을 거예요). ㄹ-final stems attach -ㄹ 거예요 directly (살다 → 살 거예요). For first-person use with intention; for third-person it expresses inference about the future. Contrast with V-(으)ㄹ게요 (first-person promise/commitment only) and A/V-겠- (volition or inference based on sensory evidence). V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 is the general-purpose future and is also used for inference (third person).

entries.shortExplanation: V이/히/리/기다 (passive) means "lexical passive verbs" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V이/히/리/기다 (passive) (Vi/hi/ri/gida (passive)) means "lexical passive verbs" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 문이 닫혔어요. ("The door was closed."). Four suffixes attach to specific verb stems to create passive verbs: -이- (보다 → 보이다, 쓰다 → 쓰이다), -히- (읽다 → 읽히다, 잡다 → 잡히다), -리- (팔다 → 팔리다, 듣다 → 들리다), -기- (안다 → 안기다, 막다 → 막히다).

entries.shortExplanation: V이/히/리/기/우/추/구다 (causative) means "lexical causative verbs" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "lexical causative verbs" uses the pattern V이/히/리/기/우/추/구다 (causative) (Vi/hi/ri/gi/u/chu/guda (causative)). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹였어요. entries.shortExplanation: N에게 / 한테 / 께 means "to / from a person" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N에게 / 한테 / 께 (Nege / hante / kke) = "to / from a person". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 친구에게 문자를 보냈어요. ("I sent a text to a friend."). Attach directly to a noun. 에게 is written/formal; 한테 is colloquial; 께 is honorific. Direction 'to': 친구에게 편지를 써요. Direction 'from': add 서 to the dative — 에게서 / 한테서 / 께서. For non-person recipients use N에 not N에게. Distinguish N에게서 (from a person) from N에서 (from a place). The particle 한테 is identical in function to 에게 but is conversational — do not use in formal writing.

entries.shortExplanation: N밖에 + 부정 means "nothing but / only with negation" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "nothing but / only with negation" uses the pattern N밖에 + 부정 (Nbakke + bujeong). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 돈이 천 원밖에 없어요. ("I only have 1,000 won."). Attach 밖에 directly to a noun. The predicate MUST be negative: 없다, 안 V, 못 V, V지 않다. N밖에 없어요 = 'there is only N / nothing but N'. Using 밖에 with a positive predicate is ungrammatical. Contrast with N만 (only N, takes a positive predicate). N밖에 emphasizes scarcity or restriction — the speaker feels the amount is insufficient. 밖에 없다 is very common and should be memorized as a chunk.

entries.shortExplanation: -군요 / -구나 means "realization / exclamation ending" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: -군요 / -구나 (-gunyo / -guna) = "realization / exclamation ending". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 그렇군요. 몰랐어요. ("Oh, I see. I didn't know that."). Polite form: verb/adjective stem + 군요. For action verbs in present tense add 는 before 군요: V-는군요. For descriptive verbs attach directly: A-군요. Casual/intimate form: -구나. Past: V/A-았/었군요. Expresses the speaker's sudden realization or surprise — often a monologue-type exclamation. Contrast with -네요 (pattern-113): -네요 is more common in everyday speech and implies direct sensory discovery; -군요 is slightly more literary/formal. -구나 is used in casual speech or when talking to oneself / to a child. 그렇군요 is a very common filler meaning 'I see / is that so?'.

entries.shortExplanation: N만 means "only / just" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "only / just" uses the pattern N만 (Nman). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 저만 왔어요. ("Only I came."). Attach 만 directly to the noun. It replaces 은/는/이/가/을/를 but follows place/time particles: 여기서만 'only here'. Contrast with 밖에: 만 can appear in positive sentences, 밖에 cannot. 만 is neutral — it does not express surprise or judgment about the quantity. Compare: 물만 마셔요 (I drink only water, neutral) vs. 물밖에 못 마셔요 (I can drink nothing but water, implies restriction/hardship).

entries.shortExplanation: V-았/었으면 좋겠어요 (counterfactual wish) means "counterfactual wish" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "counterfactual wish" uses the pattern V-았/었으면 좋겠어요 (counterfactual wish) (V-at/eosseumyeon jokesseoyo (counterfactual wish)). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 좀 더 일찍 알았으면 좋겠어요. ("I wish I had known a bit earlier."). Past tense marker + -으면. With 좋겠어요: expresses a wish that something were different now (simple counterfactual wish). Despite the past morpheme, refers to present or future unmet conditions. Stronger than present 으면 좋겠어요, which can express open future hopes. Contrast with V-았/었더라면 (pattern-153, stronger counterfactual with stated regret and result clause). 았/었으면 좋겠어요 is a complete sentence by itself; 았/었더라면 typically pairs with -았/었을 텐데 or -았/었을 거예요.

entries.shortExplanation: V-았/었더라면 … -았/었을 텐데 means "strong counterfactual conditional" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-았/었더라면 … -았/었을 텐데 (V-at/eotdeoramyeon … -at/eosseul tende) = "strong counterfactual conditional". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 그때 포기하지 않았더라면 지금쯤 성공했을 텐데. ("If I hadn't given up then, I would probably be successful by now."). Past marker + -더라면: strongly counterfactual, implies the condition was definitively not met.

entries.shortExplanation: V-기 vs V-는 것 (nominalisation contrast) means "nominalization contrast" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: V-기 vs V-는 것 (nominalisation contrast) (V-gi vs V-neun geot (nominalisation contrast)) means "nominalization contrast" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 운동하기 어렵지만 계속하고 있어요. ("Exercising is difficult, but I keep at it. 기 + 어렵다"). Select -기 for abstract or predicate-selected contexts: after 좋아하다, 싫어하다, 바라다, 원하다, 시작하다, 그만두다, 어렵다, 쉽다, and after postpositions 위해, 전에, 때문에.

Stronger surprise or exclamation than 네요; often used when the speaker is more visibly impressed or realising something significant.

entries.shortExplanation: N이/가 vs N은/는 (discourse contrast) means "topic versus subject particles" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: N이/가 vs N은/는 (discourse contrast) (Ni/ga vs Neun/neun (discourse contrast)) = "topic versus subject particles". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 어제 친구가 전화했어요. ("A friend called yesterday. — new info: the call-maker is the friend"). Use 이/가 when the noun phrase is new to the discourse, answers an implicit 'who/what' question, or exhaustively identifies the subject ('It is specifically N and not others').

entries.shortExplanation: 즉 / 다시 말해서 (written clarification) means "written clarification connectors" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: 즉 / 다시 말해서 (written clarification) (jeuk / dasi malhaeseo (written clarification)) = "written clarification connectors". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 이 계획은 비용이 너무 많이 든다. 즉, 현실적이지 않다는 뜻이다. ("This plan costs too much. That is, it is not realistic."). 즉 ('that is, namely') introduces a restatement or specification of the previous clause.

entries.shortExplanation: 결국 / 궁극적으로 (culmination markers) means "culmination markers" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: 결국 / 궁극적으로 (culmination markers) (gyeolguk / gunggeukjeogeuro (culmination markers)) means "culmination markers" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 결국 중요한 것은 노력이다. ("In the end, what matters is effort."). 결국 ('in the end, ultimately') summarises a chain of events or arguments.

entries.shortExplanation: ㅋㅋ / ㅠㅠ / ㅇㅇ (consonant emoticons) means "Korean consonant emoticons" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: "Korean consonant emoticons" uses the pattern ㅋㅋ / ㅠㅠ / ㅇㅇ (consonant emoticons) (kk / yuyu / ngng (consonant emoticons)). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 그거 진짜요? ㅋㅋㅋ ("Is that real? haha / lol"). Laughter, distress, and affirmation expressed through single consonants or consonant repetition in informal digital communication.

entries.english: liaison: final consonant links to a following vowel
entries.shortExplanation: 연음: 받침 + 모음 means "liaison: final consonant links to a following vowel" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: 연음: 받침 + 모음 (yeoneum: batchim + moeum) means "liaison: final consonant links to a following vowel" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 먹어요 → [머거요] ("먹어요 is pronounced as 머거요."). When a syllable-final consonant is followed directly by a vowel-initial syllable, the final consonant moves into the next syllable in pronunciation.

entries.shortExplanation: 비음화: ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㄴ/ㅁ means "nasalization before ㄴ or ㅁ" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: 비음화: ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㄴ/ㅁ (bieumhwa: g/d/b + n/m) = "nasalization before ㄴ or ㅁ". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 국민 → [궁민] ("국민 is pronounced 궁민."). Before nasal sounds ㄴ or ㅁ, stop codas often become nasal: ㄱ sounds like ㅇ, ㄷ sounds like ㄴ, and ㅂ sounds like ㅁ.

entries.shortExplanation: 격음화: 받침 + ㅎ means "aspiration when stops meet ㅎ" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
entries.explanation: 격음화: 받침 + ㅎ (gyeogeumhwa: batchim + h) means "aspiration when stops meet ㅎ" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 좋다 → [조타] ("좋다 is pronounced 조타."). When ㅎ meets ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅈ across a syllable boundary, the result is usually the aspirated sound ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, or ㅊ.
